items.title: Taylor Swift’s Audience Is Growing Up. Her Music Is Devolving.
items.description: Some music pulls you out of yourself, jolting you with the recognition that the person who’s singing is just as complex as you are. Some music gets you to surrender to the fact that you’re merely an overgrown baby who responds to repetition and rhyme. And some music strands you in a state of embarrassment at the human condition. Taylor Swift has lately been making music in that last category, and the discomfort is reaching terminal levels. On Friday, she released four new tracks for The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore , the deluxe edition of her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl . Bonus tracks are usually thought of as, well, bonuses—treats for the fans and incidental to an artist’s arc. But the reaction this time has drawn so much disgust that it’s like Swift mailed a horse’s head to each of her listeners. Swift has long led a cultural turn toward revaluing feelings and sounds that were once thought of as childish—but now her audience seems restless to grow up. Produced by the factory-precise hitmakers Max Martin and Shellback, Showgirl was billed as her return to pure pop after an experimental detour on 2024’s The Tortured Poets Department . Showgirl enjoyed the best-selling first week in music history—not because it amazed the broadest audience possible but because it goaded superfans to buy multiple copies . Some of those fans began to grumble that their idol was taking them for granted. Showgirl ’s music mostly felt like a bad sitcom: brightly toned but cynically spirited, verbose but charmless. When Swift announced deluxe tracks last week after posting a photo of herself in an austere cocktail dress, it seemed possible she’d taken the public feedback and refined Showgirl ’s fluffy, empty aesthetic. Alas, no. Encore does contain some intriguing ideas: strings on “Patient Zero” that sound like they’re playing from the walls of Enya’s castle, a sensitive and somewhat mysterious character study on “Babylon.” But, as on the original Showgirl , the music is too stiff to soar. Verses evoke “Baby Shark” with blocky melodies that overly emphasize each rhyming syllable. Her lyrics, usually laden with double and triple meanings, invite little extended analysis. Sometimes she raps like a funky uncle delivering a wedding toast. The worst offender is “Cleveland!” Pattering like a musical-theater sidekick, she complains about haters who make fun of her dancing and her looks, until the chorus announces that everything’s fine because her man loves her. Perky piano and glockenspiel imitate ecstatic classics such as Commodores’ “Easy” and Sufjan Stevens’s “Chicago” in the same way that stick figures imitate human beings. The problem isn’t that she sounds happy, and neither is it that she’s nah-nah-nah ing at critics for the zillionth time in her career. It’s that the song hits the same note (literally, figuratively, lyrically, musically) over and over. Listening feels like getting beaten with a candy cane. Swift’s stans are notorious for their loyalty, but online, the consensus around Encore is harsh. “I’m a Swiftie and Even I Think These New Songs Are Terrible,” the headline of Poppie Platt’s review in The Telegraph reads. The superfan-slash- critic who goes by the name Swiftologist recorded a reaction in which his voice cracked as he said, “It’s so hard to be the Swiftologist at a time like this!” One strain of backlash has centered on the notion that she’s too old to be making music this simplistic . On X, someone posted her lyrics with a picture of Sex and the City ’s Samantha saying, “If you were 25, that would be adorable, but you’re 32, so that’s just stupid.” Swift will turn 37 in December. This line of critique is a little surprising given how Swift has long subverted expectations about her age and gender. As a teenager, she wrote songs that weren’t so much wise beyond her years as reflective of the truth that young people have brains and use them. “Fifteen,” released when she was 18, empathized with and advised girls just a few years younger than her; on “22,” she both celebrated and mocked her own 22-year-old giddiness. In titling her hit 2014 album 1989 , after her birth year, she practically insisted that she be seen as the consummate Millennial. As she got older, her anxieties as a 30-something in a field that loves to discard older women became a source of inspiration: She sang on 2022’s “Anti-Hero” that she felt like a “monster on a hill” next to the “sexy baby” singers coming up behind her. Her music itself has suggested a deep rethinking of what it means to mature. Reconciling complex storytelling and catchy melodies in fresh and clever ways with each release , Swift has conveyed that growing older needn’t mean ditching the pleasures inherent to pop. Neither does it mean discarding the vulnerability, the self-interest, and the swooning that are typically seen as teenager fare. This proved influential at a time when childhood and adulthood were colliding in so many corners of culture—with shorts at the office , comic-book movies at the Oscars, and stuffed animals on adult backpacks . In the 21st century, pop culture doesn’t ask grown-ups to put away childish things; it urges them to upgrade them, remix them, and vest them with new importance to suit each phase of life. [ Read: How did Taylor Swift convince the world that she’s relatable? ] But lately the civilizationally ominous problems with clinging to youth are starting to seem glaring. Surgery and skin care in the pursuit of dewiness are warping people’s relationship with their own face . America’s romance recession has the air of a cooties panic. Democracy has been destabilized by the schoolyard-bully stylings of Donald Trump and his propagandists posting anime from official White House accounts. Last year, the musician Patrick Cosmos proposed a “new unified theory of American reality” called “everyone is twelve now.” The theory went viral because it really did seem to explain such disparate phenomena as Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s meaty diet and Emerald Fennell’s slimy, silly Wuthering Heights . At some point, a cultural countermovement calling back to earlier ideals of adulthood—restraint, nuance, care for the collective—seems likely to catch on. In music, that turn may be under way already. The breakout soul singer Olivia Dean, at age 27, projects the calm sophistication of last century’s torch singers. The country star Ella Langley just smashed the record for the longest-running Hot 100 No. 1 with music that emanates seen-it-all, world-weary wisdom (she’s also 27). In August, at Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival, a class of singers that’s been tagged as “girly pop” organized a serious-minded and historically informed effort for abortion rights and women’s health. Even music’s recent confrontation over Israel and Palestine resembles a coming-of-age crisis: Ed Sheeran claimed that he avoided commenting on politics in deference to kids in his audience, but eventually, the pressure to speak was so great that he took a stand. Maybe it’s wishful thinking to glean a trend from those examples, but the simple truth is that time imparts lessons even to those who seem to resist aging. At the MTV VMAs on Sunday, where Swift debuted her “Patient Zero” video (a pulpy romantic-horror clip starring Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson), many accolades went to another icon who’s navigated the seasons of life in her own way: Madonna. Although the 68-year-old singer’s commitment to singing about sex and dancing in corsets leads many critics to hold her up as a sad example of not acting one’s age, really she’s shown how an aversion to compromise can keep a career viable over decades. In 1998, at age 39, she released Ray of Light , an album that saw her evolve her lyrical purview—to matters of the soul and society—as she pushed her sound in lush, yet still clubby, directions. This year, she put out Confessions II , a fan-adored album of dance bangers that also managed to deliver a forthright statement about memory and mortality. Swift’s fans, meanwhile, are exchanging theories for why she’s gone Benjamin Button . One popular (but dubious) explanation is that after marrying Travis Kelce, she’s too happy to make interesting music. Another is that everything she’s doing is “satire” (okay, but is it good?). But maybe Swift just made a strategic call after noticing how jejune pop culture has become—and in doing so, underestimated her audience. Undying support for a pop star is a fundamentally childish behavior, and although Swift’s audience still craves her brand of bubblegum confessionalism, they also expect at least the level of sophistication that she’s shown before. And at a time when so much else is regressing, artists’ role is to show us what moving forward might look like.

items.title: A Most Trumpian Plan to Make Nice With Russia
items.description: A few months ago, Donald Trump’s envoy to Eastern Europe came to the president with a new idea for breaking the deadlock in U.S. relations with Moscow. The plan involved a quid pro quo reminiscent of the Cold War: The Kremlin would free some political prisoners, and the United States would reward their release by easing sanctions on the Russian economy. Trump signed on. This new initiative, which is still in its early stages and has not been previously reported, promises to advance several of Trump’s goals at once. It would help reintegrate Russia into the global economy and broaden Trump’s talks with the Kremlin beyond the intractable war in Ukraine, which his envoys have failed to end after more than a year of diplomacy. It would create a path for the U.S. to sign lucrative deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals, and other commodities. As a bonus, the release of prisoners on humanitarian grounds could bolster Trump’s case for his long-coveted Nobel Peace Prize. This fresh approach to dealing with the Kremlin, however, is likely to outrage the Ukrainians, the Europeans, and even many of Trump’s allies on Capitol Hill. Any potential business deal between the U.S. and Russia would risk funneling money to the Russian military even as it continues to terrorize Ukraine and threatens a wider war against U.S. allies in Europe. Earlier this month, Trump signed a law co-authored by Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator, authorizing Trump to impose severe sanctions on Russia and its trading partners. Even against that backdrop, Trump’s diplomatic envoys have been quietly looking for ways to ease U.S. sanctions and do business with Moscow. John Coale, the envoy who proposed the new strategy involving the release of political prisoners, has spent more than a year testing it in Belarus, Russia’s closest ally. In talks with that country’s dictator, Alexander Lukashenko, Coale won the release of hundreds of prisoners from Belarusian jails. In exchange, the U.S. has eased its sanctions on Lukashenko’s regime and pursued a deal to buy his country’s most valuable export, a type of fertilizer known as potash. With Trump’s blessing, Coale has now set out to try the same trick with Vladimir Putin in Russia. Last week, Trump announced that the U.S. is negotiating a “massive” potash deal with Belarus. Coale, a former lawyer to Trump, told me that Russia is also a part of those negotiations. Since the start of the war in Ukraine, the U.S. has avoided trade deals involving Russia. This one would mark a rare exception if finalized. In Coale’s view, it would also help advance the cause of peace. “All this stuff works toward the possibility of peace,” Coale told me. “The more interaction, the more trade-offs—either economic, prisoners, or whatever—leads step by step toward, hopefully, peace. That’s kind of the mission.” The Ukrainians see it differently. Belarus has served as a Russian staging ground for the invasion of Ukraine, and Lukashenko has provided the Russian military with bases, supplies, and ammunition. During his visit to New York last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told me he would try his best to “block” any attempt to lift the sanctions on Russia before the war ends. “But it’s difficult,” he conceded. The Russian economy is roughly 10 times larger than Ukraine’s. “It’s very difficult to compare with Russian money, with their business.” E ver since Putin first sent troops into Ukraine, in 2014, the U.S. and Europe have used just about every variety of sanction to punish Russia for its attacks, targeting Moscow’s political elites, its industrial base, its banking system, its energy sector, and other sources of money and technology that Putin needs to wage the war. Trump temporarily eased some of those sanctions this spring, when he allowed Russia to sell more fuel on the global market, hoping to alleviate the oil-price shock caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Ukraine denounced that decision at the time. In his speech last week to the United Nations General Assembly, Zelensky again urged the West to intensify and enforce its sanctions on Russia, including the new measures Trump signed into law this month. “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time,” he said. In reference to Putin, he added: “Limit his money. Limit his war.” [ Read: The abandonment of Ukraine ] But the American negotiators have taken a softer approach, seeking to pacify Putin with the promise of economic growth. After his visit to the Kremlin earlier this month, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner described the money to be made on the back of a peace deal. He told the audience at a conference in Kyiv that business deals—or, as he called them, “prosperity agreements”—form an essential part of Trump’s strategy. If they agree to a cease-fire, Putin and Zelensky “need to have something to look forward to” in terms of foreign investment and higher living standards for their citizens. “I think that’s what gets the societies invested and excited about peace,” Kushner said via video link at the Yalta European Strategy conference. “Also it becomes, in some ways, your best security guarantee.” Ukrainians, of course, have plenty of reasons to be excited about peace apart from the prospect of higher wages. The casualty count in this war has topped 2 million people, killed and wounded, on both sides, and Russia continues to bombard Ukrainian cities day and night. Ukraine has responded with a campaign of strikes against various targets in Russia, particularly its oil refineries and other energy infrastructure. As part of any peace deal, Zelensky has demanded ironclad security guarantees from his Western allies to ensure that Russia does not attack again in the future. His negotiators told me that they do not see “prosperity agreements” with Russia as any kind of security guarantee for Ukraine. Quite the opposite: They see Western trade with Russia as a way for Putin to strengthen his military and continue the war. In recent weeks, Ukrainians have been dismayed to hear Trump’s envoys use peace negotiations as a means of advancing business deals. “This is the thing that drives them now,” one of the negotiators told me of the Americans. A second negotiator added: “They believe in the magic of business. They think that if they make these business deals, the Russians will not lapse back into militarism” after the war. As of now, the second negotiator added, Trump’s envoys do not see a way to do business with Russia without first achieving at least a partial cease-fire in Ukraine. But Coale’s strategy offers a possible work-around. The release of Russian political prisoners could give the U.S. a reason to ease sanctions, creating space for the financial transactions that Trump would like to pursue with the Russians. In Coale’s view, such deals could help bring the Ukraine war closer to a cease-fire by easing tensions between Russia and the West. “Economic ties usually result in normality,” he told me. C oale’s proposal emerged from a meeting he had this spring with a Russian dissident, Dmitry Muratov, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his decades of journalism and human-rights activism. The newspaper that Muratov co-founded and edited for many years, Novaya Gazeta , was forced to shut down soon after Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. Since then, Muratov has devoted most of his time to speaking out against the war and trying to free the Russian activists imprisoned for opposing it. Over the past year, he has closely followed reports of Coale’s work in Belarus, which I have written about at length . Coale and other U.S. diplomats have secured the release of about 500 political prisoners in Belarus, including a few American citizens. At the end of last year, Muratov asked me for an introduction to Coale. The dissident wanted to see whether Trump’s envoy could make the same appeals to the Kremlin as he had in Minsk. The release of prisoners, Muratov argued, has long been a part of American diplomacy in Moscow. At summits with Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, President Ronald Reagan or his envoys would often present the Soviets with lists of imprisoned dissidents and ask for their release. Gorbachev routinely obliged, creating a humanitarian dimension to his broader efforts to ease tensions with the Americans and reduce the risk of nuclear war. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, in 1991, Gorbachev and Muratov co-founded Novaya Gazeta and, over the years, it became Russia’s leading source of investigative reporting about the Kremlin’s abuses of power. Several of its journalists, including the legendary war reporter Anna Politkovskaya, have been murdered for their work. Before his death, in August 2022, at the age of 91, Gorbachev gave Muratov some of his possessions as keepsakes, including a commemorative medallion that Reagan gave to the Soviet leader at one of their summits. In May, Muratov brought the medallion to Washington and presented it to Coale as a token of admiration for his efforts in Belarus. Over plates of sushi at Ned’s Club, a members’ club popular among the political cognoscente, he told Trump’s envoy about the history of prisoner releases during the Cold War and the urgent need to revive this practice between the U.S. and Russia. Muratov brought photos of several of the dissidents whom Russia had jailed for their opposition to the war, and he told Coale their stories. He brought up the poet and theater director Evgenia Berkovich, who had picketed against the war in 2022. A Russian military court later sentenced her and her friend, the playwright Svetlana Petriychuk, to six years in prison on terrorism charges, part of a Kremlin campaign to criminalize any opposition to the war. Hundreds of people have been jailed in Russia for such offenses, some given years of incarceration for deeds as trivial as questioning the war in a comment on social media. Coale, for his part, described to Muratov the joy he felt the first time he managed to free a group of prisoners in Belarus last year. The experience gave the lawyer a new sense of purpose, he said, and he agreed to try a similar approach with the Russians. Soon after the meeting, Coale raised the idea with Trump, who gave his consent to try it, Coale told me. Yesterday, the White House nominated Coale to serve as the special presidential envoy for hostage affairs, with the rank of ambassador, a role that will require Senate confirmation. Asked to comment on his mission, a White House official said: “The President and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done.” Coale plans to coordinate his efforts with Steve Witkoff, who serves as Trump’s main point of contact with the Russians. A billionaire real-estate developer with no formal diplomatic experience, Witkoff has met with Putin at least seven times since the start of the war in Ukraine. During his most recent visit to the Kremlin, on September 5, the Russian leader expressed his gratitude to Witkoff and Kushner for their attempts to negotiate a peace deal. “I’d like to tell you that we find it comfortable to work with you, and, of course, we have a very high level of trust during this work,” Putin told the two Americans, according to footage of the meeting published on the Kremlin website. In response, Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing an American teacher, Bob Gilman, who had been jailed in Russia since 2022. Their conversation then shifted to the war in Ukraine. Kushner and Witkoff planned to fly from Moscow to Kyiv via Poland the next day, according to two people familiar with their travel arrangements. Neither of the American envoys had visited Ukraine during the war. As part of their preparations, Putin said, the Americans had requested a three-day cease-fire to allow the trip to proceed safely, and the Russians had given their consent. “I issued the respective order,” Putin said, adding that, since midnight that day, no strikes had been carried out on Kyiv. This appears to have been a lie. That morning, a Russian drone struck the territory of Kyiv’s main airport, in the city of Boryspil, where Witkoff and Kushner had been due to land the following day, according to the two people familiar with their travel plans. One of them, a Ukrainian official, showed me surveillance footage of the strike and photos of the crater it left near the runway. After the attack—which took place at 9:12 a.m. on September 5, while Kushner and Witkoff were flying to Moscow—the Americans changed their plans for the next day and traveled to Kyiv from Poland by train, the two people familiar with their trip told me. [ Read: Putin is slipping into delusion ] (The drone strike on Boryspil and its consequences have not been previously reported. A U.S. official familiar with the trip denied that Kushner and Witkoff changed their plans because of the airport attack but said that, in general, their travel arrangements often shift on short notice.) When informed of their need to reach Kyiv by train, the Ukrainian railway company scrambled to prepare a luxury cabin for the U.S. delegation, complete with a spread of Tatar cuisine from Crimea and a little sign on the dining table that said Peace arrives on time . A fter arriving in Kyiv, Kushner and Witkoff met for several hours with Zelensky and his team of negotiators. Two of them later told me that the talks focused on a variety of ways to achieve a limited cease-fire, which could be expanded into a broader peace deal to end the war in stages. “Their whole message right now is to shrink the conflict, in any way, from any direction,” one of the negotiators said of the Americans. Next month, he said, they aim to organize a gathering of envoys from the U.S., Russia, and Ukraine, most likely in Abu Dhabi, to discuss a limited cease-fire. It could oblige each side not to strike the other’s energy infrastructure, including power plants, oil refineries, and similar targets. A separate deal, mediated with help from the government of Egypt, would call for Russia and Ukraine not to strike one another’s cargo ships in the Black Sea, particularly those carrying grain to markets in the Middle East and Africa, the negotiators told me. The Americans have been keen to arrange a meeting with Trump, Putin, and Zelensky as soon as possible. On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. had invited Putin to the G20 summit to be held in December, at Trump’s golf club in Miami, where Trump could also try to bring Zelensky to the table. Putin has yet to accept the invitation. Regardless of the venue and format, Zelensky would be eager to participate in such a summit, one of his close aides told me: “He still has this idea that he can look Putin in the eyes and figure this out.” Putin has shown no such inclination. Although he seemed happy to host Kushner and Witkoff at the Kremlin this month, Russian attacks on Kyiv and other cities have grown deadlier and more frequent in recent weeks. For the first time since the start of the war, Russia has begun launching regular daytime strikes against the Ukrainian capital, killing or wounding scores of civilians, forcing businesses to close and schools to hold classes in bomb shelters. Two days before Kushner and Witkoff arrived in Kyiv, a Russian drone slammed into the headquarters of Ukraine’s main intelligence agency and exploded inside the office of its director. He survived the strike, but the Ukrainians saw it as a major escalation and a sign of Russia’s plans for the next few months. None of the handful of officials in Zelensky’s administration who spoke with me for this article expected Putin to engage in any serious peace talks until the spring at the earliest. “He has been stockpiling missiles for a reason, and he intends to use them this winter,” one of them told me. Given that lack of will on the Russian side, the flurry of peace talks initiated by Trump’s envoys in recent weeks has felt like a waste of time to some of the participants. As one of them described it to me the other day, “It almost feels like we’re all just dancing around Putin, offering him this and that, whatever we can think of, but he’s not moving.” C oale’s plan would seek to break that impasse. The issue of political prisoners, once introduced into the dialogue between the U.S. and Russia, would give Putin an easy way to demonstrate goodwill and create fresh signs of diplomatic progress with the Americans while continuing to terrorize Ukraine. Last month’s release of Gilman, the American teacher, serves as a case in point, and Coale told me that he has already gathered a list of other Americans held in Russian prisons. A separate list, compiled with help from Muratov, will include dissidents, journalists, and others incarcerated for their opposition to the war. Trade and business talks would run parallel to these discussions, and one business deal has already demonstrated how they could work, expanding the points of contact between the U.S. and Russia beyond the peace talks in Ukraine, Coale told me. Last Tuesday, Trump announced on Truth Social that the U.S. was working on “a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” adding that it would be “very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.” That deal resulted in large part from Coale’s work. In response to the release of political prisoners, the U.S. lifted some of its sanctions on that country’s regime to allow the deal to proceed. The discussions also involve Russia, Coale explained. European countries have not agreed to ease their own sanctions on Belarus, and they have refused to allow the transport of potash from Belarus across their territory. That means it would most likely need to move eastward through Russia before reaching international markets, making the Kremlin a party to the deal. [ Read: The irreversible change in Belarus ] “If the West is buying potash, then they’ve got to deal with the Russians and the Belarusians. So you’re sitting down at a table, and you’re haggling over price or finding the routes to get it out,” Coale told me. “When people talk, it’s a good thing. Even if they’re talking about potash, it may go into having the countries, as I say, going back to the family of nations with the rest of the world.” Coale said his strategy would not abandon Ukraine, but it would seek to strengthen ties between the U.S. and Russia, encouraging Putin to end the war as part of a broader agenda of business and trade with the West. By switching from the stick of sanctions to the carrot of mutual profits, this plan follows a lesson Coale learned last year from Putin’s closest ally, the Belarusian dictator Lukashenko. “In the name of peace, maybe you’ve got to be a little cunning and make some concessions,” Lukashenko told me last August, describing the advice he gave Coale for dealing with the Kremlin. “Even if you can’t make sense of Putin, treat him like a human being.” As the U.S. began easing sanctions on Belarus last year, Lukashenko helped the Americans arrange a summit with Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, where Trump greeted the Russian leader on a red carpet. Their talks did not result in any breakthrough in the efforts to end the war in Ukraine. On the contrary, Russia only intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s power plants, apartment blocks, and other civilian targets. But the Alaska summit did ease the diplomatic isolation of Ukraine’s main adversaries. On his flight to Anchorage aboard Air Force One, Trump called Lukashenko to thank him for releasing political prisoners and, in a post on social media, referred to the despot as a “Highly Respected President.” Ever since, Coale has continued working with Lukashenko to win the release of prisoners and negotiate business deals. His approach has alarmed many diplomats in Europe, who have called on the U.S. to maintain its sanctions pressure on Belarus and Russia. The leader of the democratic opposition in Belarus, Svetlana Tikhanovskaya, told me last week that the exchange of prisoners for sanctions relief will only encourage the regimes in Russia and Belarus to take more prisoners. “This trade in human beings costs them nothing,” she said during her visit to New York for the UN General Assembly. “They can always arrest more people, while the West loses its leverage over these regimes by lifting sanctions and making deals.” Tikhanovskaya’s own husband, a prominent blogger in Belarus who tried to run for president against the country’s dictator in 2020, was freed from prison last year in a release that Coale negotiated with the regime. When I pointed out the contradiction in Tikhanovskaya’s stance, she struggled for a moment to explain it. Her family, which now lives in exile, had been reunited thanks to the Trump administration’s strategy of swapping economic deals for foreign detainees. Yet she now argues that the families of other political prisoners should not benefit from such trades. “I know it seems unfair,” she said finally. “But if we do this, in Russia or in Belarus, those regimes will take more hostages, and their families will go through the same horrors that we did.” Muratov’s stance on this dilemma bears an even greater irony. He lives in Moscow, and the prominence bestowed on him by the Nobel Peace Prize would make him a valuable prisoner for the Kremlin to trade away. Russian authorities recently began investigating his taxes, which could give the Kremlin an easy excuse to put Muratov in jail and offer him up to the Americans in exchange for sanctions relief. But the dissident does not seem deterred by that risk. If Coale’s campaign frees the innocent people already jailed in Russia for speaking out against the war, Muratov told me, it will have been worth it for them and their families, even if the story ends with him in a prison cell. Ashley Parker contributed reporting to this article.

items.title: The Art of Dealing With Trump
items.description: T he best metaphor for trade negotiations may be trying to arrange a marriage. Countries come to the table with friendly intentions, hoping to form a partnership. The pressure is to make a deal, not to block one, and if they don’t succeed, that is a cause for sorrow, not anger. Donald Trump has changed all of that. He has turned trade deals from negotiations about marriage to threats of divorce. Before Trump, the Western consensus had long been that free trade made individual countries richer overall, and the world richer too. Trump does not believe that. More importantly, his trade negotiations aren’t only, or even mostly, about trade. They are about domestic politics and geopolitics, and, above all, they are about staging a drama in which he, and America, wins. Trump is trying to turn trade from a win-win relationship to a battle for dominance over adversaries and a protection racket for friends. This is trade policy as per Roald Dahl’s Matilda rather than Adam Smith. The organizing principle for this MAGA administration is that countries need to pay for the right to sell things to the United States. They can pay quite literally, through tariffs. They can pay by pledging investments in the U.S. And they can pay with actions that have no connection to trade but that the White House wants. Most of America’s allies have simply capitulated—accepting harmful and unjust tariffs or offering other forms of tribute. [ Read: Why Trump has it out for Canada ] My experience as Canada’s international trade minister and foreign minister during the first Trump administration suggests another possible strategy. A decade ago, Trump threatened to tear up the North American Free Trade Agreement and destroy Canada’s most important trade relationship. Canada was gobsmacked, but we were also prepared. In the summer of 2016, our ambassador began to warn us that Trump might win. So I asked our outstanding trade officials to prepare a memo outlining what we should do if a victorious Trump carried through on his campaign-trail attacks on NAFTA. We called it the “in emergency, break glass” briefing note. In the days after the election, that homework paid off. Canada was angry, but we also stayed calm. We met Trump and his team at the table, looked for things we could agree about, and held firm to our red lines. Throughout two years of negotiation, Trump and his minions insulted and demeaned Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and me, calling me a “nasty woman” who “hates America.” In 2018, he imposed illegal and unjustified tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. Canada then did something that much of the world has forgotten how to do: We fought back, with dollar-for-dollar reciprocal tariffs. Because ultimately, the only thing that works with this president is strength. During our years of negotiating, we developed a three-part playbook for handling the Trump administration. It eventually got us to a great deal, and it can help America’s allies deal with the White House today. First: Look for areas where you agree and can work together. Second, apply the doughnut strategy: Yes, the president is important, but he is just one figure in the middle of a big country. Be sure to talk with Americans in the rest of the doughnut, not just in the Oval Office in the middle. Third, and most important: Do not capitulate. D uring the NAFTA negotiations , we shuttled back and forth to Washington more than a dozen times. The talks were high drama. Sometimes the Americans yelled at us; at other times, they graciously served us snacks, including Hershey’s Kisses with packaging signed by Donald Trump. As we waited in the White House for a bilateral meeting between the president and the prime minister, a smiling, jocular Gary Cohn, a senior economic aide to Trump at the time, once told me: “You’re definitely going to get screwed. The only question is whether you get screwed with a kiss.” Occasionally, I would take refuge in the ladies’ washroom—generally a safe space, because there were usually no women on the U.S. side of the table. Once, at a particularly dire moment, I got down on my knees there and prayed. Holding your ground when Trump demands that you buckle is not easy. Political rivals accused our team of “Napping on NAFTA” and said we should accept more of Trump’s proposals. In response, I said then what I believe now: “Capitulation is not a negotiating strategy.” This article has been adapted from Chrystia Freeland’s new book, Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider’s View of Dealing With a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People . That doesn’t preclude finding areas of agreement. Trump lies so much about trade that it can be hard to recognize when he has a point. But the fact is that the old NAFTA, and the free-trade consensus it represented, really did have problems. For example, Trump was right that the low wages paid to Mexican auto workers undermined American workers, especially in the states that had gotten him elected in 2016. We had dealt with similar concerns when negotiating an earlier trade deal between Canada and the European Union: European socialists, much like American right-wing populists, wanted deals that supported high wages for workers and that protected national sovereignty against multinational corporations. I agreed. And that is one reason we were able to make a deal with Donald Trump. The Americans demanded that a specific quota of U.S.-made parts be included in a NAFTA-compliant car. We made a counterproposal: A certain percentage of the car had to be manufactured by workers making at least $16 an hour. This would become one of the smartest features of the new NAFTA, designed to protect the jobs that had been outsourced since the original deal while disarming American efforts to kill the Canadian auto industry. But for Trump, getting a good deal isn’t really the point. In 2018, the United States levied illegal and unjustified tariffs against Canadian steel and aluminum, claiming that our exports were a threat to U.S. national security. I pushed for retaliation, and Prime Minister Trudeau agreed. We weren’t a security threat to America; to suggest that we were was insulting. We were responding more in sorrow than in anger. But this was a big move, the largest trade retaliation Canada had imposed since the second world war. We targeted goods that would cause maximum political pain in the United States and do little damage in Canada: ketchup and jam made in Pennsylvania and Ohio, to put pressure on the president’s Rust Belt constituency; bourbon and playing cards, to make an impact in Kentucky, home to Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and the U.S. ambassador to Canada, Kelly Craft; and cheese and yogurt to pressure House Speaker Paul Ryan of Wisconsin. [ Read: Europe and Canada are like the kids in an ugly divorce ] Canada didn’t start this fight. We were simply responding, dollar for dollar, to the tariffs the U.S. had imposed on our steel and aluminum. We coordinated with Mexico and the EU to maximize our impact, and we left room for negotiation by waiting a month after U.S. tariffs went into force before imposing our own. When we announced our retaliatory action, I told Canadians that I had spoken with Robert Lighthizer, the U.S. trade representative, six times in the previous week and that Canada was willing to talk any place, any time. The mere declaration that we were going to retaliate infuriated President Trump. He started bullying Canada and Canadian leaders publicly and privately. Just as we were getting ready to unveil our final tariff list, Trump made a personal phone call to Trudeau, in which he threatened dire consequences, including destroying the Canadian auto industry, if we went through with our plan. He told Trudeau that I was a “nasty woman” who had spoken critically about him to other world leaders. Peter Navarro, the White House’s trade adviser, hastily dismissed the impact of retaliatory tariffs as little more than a “rounding error” for the U.S. economy, but Trump’s intemperance betrayed greater anxiety. Many Canadian business leaders were anxious about an all-out trade war with the United States, and at least one of my cabinet colleagues, the finance minister, argued that we should postpone our trade action beyond the one-month grace period we had already extended and just keep talking. I understood the fear. A trade fight with the United States would be more painful for us than for the Americans, as the $16.6 billion in goods targeted by the tariffs was 0.06 percent of the U.S. GDP, but 0.74 percent of ours. We also had more at stake: Trade accounts for about 65 percent of the Canadian economy, and more than 70 percent of our exports were to the United States in 2018. Trade is about 25 percent of the U.S. economy, and 18 percent of U.S. exports were to Canada in 2018. But I was absolutely certain that we needed to fight back, and I was equally confident that if we did so, we would succeed. Trump is a textbook bully. For him, weakness is a provocation. But when he is met with strength, he finds a way to make a deal. Trump doesn’t always chicken out, per the TACO meme. Just ask Nicolás Maduro. But he does find ways to change course when the other side keeps its nerve, as the dictators in Beijing and Tehran—and the Democrats in Minneapolis—have shown. The economic facts had always been on our side. Trade between Canada and the United States was balanced, mutually beneficial, and made both of our countries more secure. Our countries had been building things together since Henry Ford manufactured the first Model T, and Canada was a secure and reliable supplier of oil and electricity to the United States. The value of this partnership should have been enough to secure a deal—and it had been, for decades. But with this president, facts alone don’t matter, and a win-win outcome is a last resort. We had to prove to him that he couldn’t bully Canada, and that trade with Canada was actually in America’s national interest. Only by demonstrating painful consequences could we get back to a reciprocal relationship with our neighbor. We also knew that we needed to talk with people other than Trump. Among the Republican allies we courted, starting in 2017, was Paul Ryan, the speaker of the House, whose home state of Wisconsin exported nearly $7 billion a year to Canada. “I just like trade,” Ryan told me, saying that among partners, “Canada is the one that’s fair and balanced.” I met with Arizona Senator John McCain, who warned me that some of the tariff proposals, including those involving Canada, were “nuts, crazy, insane.” But he said that he would “lay down on the tracks” to oppose that approach and that “there’s enough Republicans who are against it.” Fewer than four weeks after our retaliatory tariffs went into effect, in July 2018, a business coalition supported by farm-state political leaders on both sides of the aisle launched a multimillion-dollar campaign called “Tariffs Hurt the Heartland.” They held 15 town halls across the Midwest and carried out three aggressive ad campaigns, including one called “Rounding Error” and one titled simply “Tariffs Are a Tax.” This political pressure on Trump, including from his own supporters, kept the talks on track through difficult weeks. It also enraged the president. But ultimately, and quite rightly, the people whose views most mattered to the administration were Americans themselves. They were the lobbyists who really counted. And that is why retaliation, together with the doughnut strategy, was so important. In arguing that tariffs and counter-tariffs couldn’t really hurt the United States because international trade was relatively unimportant to the American economy, Navarro and like-minded economists made the same mistake that globalization advocates once made. They failed to account for the pain their policy would cause specific people and specific communities. Tariffs might be a “rounding error” in aggregate, but for some people and some places, they were devastating. Ground zero for tariff pain was Iowa, a farm state where one in five jobs depended on trade. By May, coordinated retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada and other countries hurt by the U.S. had cost the state’s farmers, particularly pork and soybean producers, nearly $1.5 billion in lost export revenue. That came out to roughly $17,000 per farm. The Tariffs Hurt the Heartland campaign created an interactive map, populated with heart-wrenching stories from midwesterners. W hen President Trump took office for his second term last year, he was met with a wave of capitulation. Many American CEOs, lawyers, and university presidents bowed their heads to avoid his wrath. America’s international allies largely surrendered too—knuckling under in response to tariffs, appeasing the president at the first NATO summit, and responding to insults and ridicule during White House visits with sycophancy and fixed smiles. But America’s allies have also shown that they can stand Trump down. When Trump threatened to seize Greenland in January 2026, the EU did not give in. And Greenland remains part of the Kingdom of Denmark, following some clever diplomacy by Copenhagen, which succeeded in reaffirming its sovereignty without reigniting the war of words. [ Read: America’s allies are no longer waiting for Trump to leave ] Many of us in allied countries feel so angry, so frightened, and so betrayed right now that we easily forget how much we have prospered, together, during the American century. Pax Americana has not always been benign, of course, and living with a hegemon is often uncomfortable. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, Justin’s father, brilliantly compared sharing a border with the United States to sleeping next to an elephant: Even if the elephant is gracious and well disposed toward you, you never sleep altogether easily. A lot has changed since 2018, but I still believe two things that I believed then—that America can be a force for good in the world, and that we need to be frank with our American friends about how profoundly they are losing our trust. The official public obsequiousness that is the love language of the Oval Office, and which America is hearing from too much of the world, masks a disenchantment that is hardening into contempt. Rather than containing the president, his appeasers have enabled him. America’s allies must speak out, and they must do so together. Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is showing America’s other friends that when you stand up to a bully, you can rally your country behind you. That approach worked in 2018, and it can work today. And, ultimately, it is in America’s best interest too. By refusing to submit, we can help Americans remember that the most effective way to treat their allies—and not just authoritarian tyrants—is with partnership, not punishment. If America can relearn that lesson, which the postwar generation first taught, it will be a win-win outcome for democrats and democracies everywhere. This article has been adapted from Chrystia Freeland’s new book, Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider’s View of Dealing With a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People .

items.title: République populaire de Chine : La protection de l’environnement, une priorité de développement national
items.description: Les montagnes verdoyantes et les eaux limpides sont un trésor inestimable. Cette citation du président chinois Xi Jinping témoigne de l’intérêt accordé par les autorités chinoises à la protection de l’environnement. En effet, la protection de l'environnement est devenue une priorité de développement national en Chine. Le développement de la Chine dans les années 1980 et 1990 avait entrainé une détérioration de l'environnement. La dégradation de l'environnement était d’ailleurs un phénomène courant dans les années 1980 et 1990. Elle était même considérée comme le prix à payer pour le développement et la modernisation. Le modèle de développement de presque tous les pays d'Asie était d'abord le développement et ensuite le nettoyage. Des pays comme le Japon et la Corée du Sud étaient aussi concernés par le même phénomène. Mais dès le XXIe siècle, la Chine a accordé de l’importance à la protection de l'environnement. Le Gouvernement chinois a mis davantage l'accent sur le développement vert et a pris une série de mesures pour promouvoir le développement de l'économie verte. Le président chinois Xi Jinping : « L'homme et la nature forment une communauté de vie. Nous, en tant qu'êtres humains, devons respecter la nature, suivre ses voies et la protéger » " data-large-file="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14.jpeg" class="size-full wp-image-170982" src="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14.jpeg" alt="" width="1023" height="765" srcset="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14.jpeg 1023w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14-300x224.jpeg 300w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14-768x574.jpeg 768w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14-562x420.jpeg 562w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14-80x60.jpeg 80w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14-150x112.jpeg 150w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14-696x520.jpeg 696w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-29-at-10.23.14-265x198.jpeg 265w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1023px) 100vw, 1023px" /> Le président chinois Xi Jinping : « L'homme et la nature forment une communauté de vie. Nous, en tant qu'êtres humains, devons respecter la nature, suivre ses voies et la protéger » La Chine s’est d’abord dotée d’un Plan national de reforestation 2011–2020. Elle a également procédé à la protection des zones touchées par la désertification, à la gestion et transformation de ces domaines, au développement des activités liées au sable, ainsi qu’au renforcement des capacités, la promotion des nouvelles technologies et le renforcement du suivi. Aujourd’hui, le résultat est remarquable. Après 30 ans de transformation,1/3 du désert de Kubu (plus de 145 hectares), est devenu oasis. La forêt de Saihanba dans le Hebei qui était autrefois un désert est aujourd’hui la plus grande forêt artificielle du monde. À partir de 1962, pour protéger Pékin des tempêtes du sable, cette forêt artificielle a été construite au nord de la capitale. Le couvert forestier est passé de 12% à plus de 80% en 2016. Huzhou, le sanctuaire du bambou La transformation du plateau de Loess constitue également un grand exemple en matière de protection de l’environnement en Chine. Depuis plus de 30 ans, le plateau de Loess a été reboisé, de sorte que l'érosion a été atténuée et l'eau devient plus claire et moins jaune. Le développement de l'industrie du bambou a également constitué une mesure mise en œuvre par la Chine pour protéger son environnement. Lorsqu’on parle de bambou, c’est la ville de Huzhou qui nous vient immédiatement en tête. Située dans la province du Zhejiang, cette ville est réputée pour son industrie du bambou. Huzhou est une ville verte avec plus de 71% de couverture forestière, en particulier des forêts de bambous. Au fil des ans, les habitants ont fait de la culture du bambou leur principale ressource et ont construit plus de 6000 hectares de forêts de bambous. Il y a plus de 2000 entreprises spécialisées dans la production de matériaux, de meubles, de fibres de bambou, de nourriture de pousses de bambou, etc. Ils peuvent fabriquer plus de 3000 produits qu’ils exportent dans plus de 30 pays à travers le monde. L'industrie du bambou a bénéficié du soutien des politiques publiques à travers la création de coopératives qui favorise le développement intensif du bambou ainsi que la promotion des activités liées aux forêts de bambous, telle la culture de champignons dans les forêts de bambous, et l'élevage de poulets, etc. Dans sa politique de développement vert, la Chine a également procédé à la création de parcs nationaux pour protéger les espèces naturelles. Des espaces verts dans les mégapoles Elle a créé d’abord cinq parcs nationaux naturels avec un objectif précis, celui de protéger les espèces naturelles. Le parc naturel national dans le Nord-Est est spécialisé dans la protection de tigres et de léopards. Dans le Sud, l’île de Hainan est une forêt tropicale pluviale. Au centre de la Chine, il y a le parc pour la protection de pandas. A la source des trois grands fleuves, il y a la zone de protection des animaux sauvages et à la montagne Wuyi, il y a la zone de protection des espèces végétaux L’une des mesures également mise en œuvre par la Chine est la construction d'espaces verts dans les mégalopoles. Les espaces verts urbains ont été multipliés par cinq, avec plus de 406 espaces verts publics à Shanghai depuis 2010. Et cela se poursuivra, car la Chine construira plus de 1 000 grands espaces verts au niveau national dans le cadre du 14 e plan quinquennal. Dans la dynamique de protection de son environnement, la Chine a également opté pour des vélos et d’autres moyens de transports partagés. Elle a également développé une industrie automobile de nouvelle énergie. Le pays s’est par ailleurs fermement engagé à réduire ses émissions de carbone, avec un objectif d’atteindre le pic d’émissions de carbone en 2030 et la neutralité carbone en 2060. La Chine a développé fortement le secteur des énergies renouvelables en produisant des équipements et des installations photovoltaïques, en produisant des équipements éoliens et en testant plusieurs canaux pour les centrales nucléaires 4g. La capacité de production d'énergie renouvelable est en train d’augmenter si rapidement ces dernières années que la Chine pourrait atteindre son objectif cinq ans plus tôt que prévu. Le moins qu’on puisse dire est que la Chine constitue un véritable exemple en matière de développement vert. Comme l’a dit le président Xi Jinping, « un environnement écologique sain est le fondement essentiel pour le développement durable de l'humanité et de la société ». Nadège YAMEOGO

items.title: Finance minister kicks off talks with visiting IMF mission
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Minister for Finance and Revenue Muhammad Aurangzeb held a kick-off meeting on Tuesday with a visiting staff mission of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The IMF mission, led by Iva Petrova, is in Islamabad for the fourth review of Pakistan’s $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) arrangement and the third review of the $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF). Aurangzeb, in a virtual meeting, briefed the IMF team on the latest macroeconomic indicators, improvements in credit rating and overall investment climate amid a challenging outlook emanating from prolonged Iran conflict . On the successful conclusion of talks, Pakistan will be entitled to disbursement of about $1.2bn under the two programmes: $1bn under the EFF and $200 million under the RSF by the end of October or early November, but may require waivers from the IMF’s executive board for slippages on structural benchmarks. The authorities are in continuous breach of structural benchmarks regarding the sovereign wealth fund (SWF) law that was originally missed in March. The federal government already notified new procurement rules on Monday, two days ahead of the deadline, ie, Sept 30. The SWF law is part of the discussions with the visiting IMF team. Authorities are in breach of an end-March 2026 structural benchmark on amendments to the Sovereign Wealth Fund Act to adopt governance mechanisms and safeguards for seven state-owned enterprises (SOEs), involving an asset portfolio of about $8bn. Most of them are blue-chip entities listed on the stock exchange but remain outside normal reporting requirements. They include OGDCL, Pakistan Petroleum Limited (PPL), Mari Petr­oleum, National Bank of Pakistan (NBP), Govt Holdings, Pakistan Development Fund, and the Neelum-Jhelum Hydropower project. The amendments are pending parliamentary approval. The IMF team has been in Pakistan since Sept 23. It spent the initial days in Karachi for engagements with the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) and other stakeholders. The staff mission has so far held engagements with officials from SBP, the finance ministry, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), the Establishment Division, and the finance secretaries of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab. New procurement rules Against this backdrop, the government notified the Public Procurement Rules 2026 to promote greater transparency and competition in public procurement while keeping certain exemptions for direct contracting with SOEs and limiting the bidding to national firms. The IMF had certain reservations over the preferential treatment of SOEs for direct contracting. Rule 32 of the new rules provides that a procuring agency may engage through EPADS (E-Pak Acquisition and Disposal System, a digital system developed and enforced by the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority) to manage and administer the process of procurement in direct contracting with SOEs for the procurement of such works and services, including consultancy ser­vices, which are time-sensitive, scattered, remotely located and in the public interest or in case of urgency and provided they do not sub-let those contracts initiated prior to the commencement of the new rules continuing under the 2004 framework. The new rules make the use of EPADS mandatory for public procurement and disposal by federal procuring agencies, provide for the establishment of dedicated procurement cells, and introduce mechanisms to discourage conflicts of interest through third-party validation, evaluation, and pre-shipment inspection for large procurements. The new rules further strengthen the enforcement mechanism through the provision of blacklisting and cross-debarment, independent grievance red­ressal committees with an appellate mechanism at PPRA to clearly identify material deviations and mis-procurement, including deliberate procurement outside EPADS, failure to constitute prescribed committees, tailor-made specifications, violation of advertisement and response-time requirements, and failure to follow prescribed evaluation criteria. The rules allow other efficient methods of procurement such as gallop tendering and alternative procurement methods, including shopping and negotiated tendering, subject to specified conditions. Efficiency measures have been embedded in the framework, reducing response times, shortening standstill periods, and streamlining tender processing cycles to enable faster contract awards. The rules also emphasise sustainable procurement, encouraging inclusiveness of SMEs and marginalised groups, and aligning procurement practices with environmental policy. EFF and RSF packages Pakis­tan and the IMF had reached the 39-month $7bn aid package deal in July 2024, with the programme set to allow the country to “cement macroeconomic stability and create conditions for stronger, more inclusive and resilient growth”. In March 2025, the two sides reached a staff-level agreement (SLA) on the first biannual review of the EFF programme and on unlocking the $1.3bn RSF arrangement. Subsequently, in May that year, the IMF’s Executive Board allowed a $1bn disbursement under the EFF — bringing total released funds under the package to about $2.1bn — and also approved the RSF loan. In October 2025, the government and the Fund reached an SLA on the second review of the EFF, securing another $1bn under the programme and $200 million under the RSF after the Board’s approval in December. A Petrova-led mission held talks with Pakistan in March this year for the third review of the EFF and the second review of the RSF, but the two sides failed to reach an agreement and decided to continue negotiations. Then in May, the IMF’s Executive Board allowed Pakistan to draw about $1.1bn under the EFF and about $220m under the RSF, bringing total disbursements under the two arrangements to roughly $4.8bn. An IMF mission, also led by Petrova, last visited Pakistan from May 13 to May 20, with the visit focusing on “recent economic developments, reform implementation, and the budget strategy for fiscal year 2027”.

items.title: Les données de plus de 3 millions d'employés du Pentagone dérobées, selon les médias
items.description: Des hackers non identifies auraient pirate la base de donnees du Pentagone contenant les informations relatives au personnel, a rapporte ABC News le 29 septembre, citant des sources. Selon la chaîne americaine, les pirates auraient eu acces a des informations confidentielles concernant plus de 3 millions d'employes du ministere de la Defense. Un representant du Pentagone a declare a ABC News que cet acces non autorise se serait produit entre octobre 2025 et juillet 2026, affectant le systeme d'information du Centre de gestion des ressources humaines du ministere. Il a assure que la faille aurait ete immediatement corrigee apres sa decouverte. L'interlocuteur d'ABC News a precise que la fuite concernait 2,76 millions de personnes encore en vie et 294 000 autres personnes decedees. Parmi les donnees auxquelles les hackers auraient eu acces figuraient des numeros de securite sociale et des informations sur les postes occupes. Selon la chaîne, l'ampleur et la sensibilite de ces donnees pourraient susciter des inquietudes en matiere de securite nationale. Il a toutefois precise qu'il n'y avait pour l'instant aucune preuve indiquant que les donnees divulguees aient ete utilisees a des fins abusives. L'une des cyberattaques les plus importantes de ces derniers temps a ete celle menee par le groupe de hackers Rhysida contre l'infrastructure informatique de l'administration berlinoise. Les cybercriminels ont procede au vol debut août dernier et ont menace de divulguer les donnees si les autorites allemandes ne versaient pas une rancon de 30 bitcoins (environ deux millions d'euros). L'ultimatum n'ayant pas ete respecte, environ 1,44 million de fichiers, representant un volume total de pres de 5,8 teraoctets, ont ete mis en ligne debut septembre. Selon les medias allemands, parmi les informations divulguees figuraient des documents confidentiels concernant les infrastructures critiques et la securite dans la capitale allemande, ainsi que des plans de lutte contre les menaces chimiques, biologiques, radiologiques et nucleaires et une analyse des vulnerabilites du reseau d'approvisionnement en eau de Berlin. Le journal Bild a quant a lui averti que certaines informations pourraient presenter un interet pour des terroristes et des services de renseignement etrangers.

items.title: Jemna Connect, un espace de coworking dédié aux jeunes
items.description: Pour soutenir les jeunes et promouvoir les initiatives locales, Jemna Connect, un nouvel espace de coworking, de formation et d’échange dédié à l’accompagnement des jeunes et au développement des initiatives locales s’ouvrira le mercredi 30 septembre 2026 à Jemna, une ville oasienne du sud-ouest de la Tunisie, située entre Kebili et Douz, à la lisière du Sahara. D’une superficie de 195 m², Jemna Connect est situé dans la nouvelle zone d’extension urbaine de la Commune de Jemna, à proximité de la route régionale RR206 et du stade Kâchi. L’espace comprend une zone d’accueil, des espaces de travail individuels et collectifs, une salle dédiée aux réunions, aux formations et aux présentations, un espace de détente, des sanitaires ainsi qu’une terrasse extérieure semi-couverte. L’espace est également ouvert aux formateurs, entrepreneurs, artistes, associations et acteurs locaux, avec pour objectif de favoriser l’autonomisation des jeunes, leur participation au développement local et l’émergence de nouvelles initiatives. La cérémonie d’inauguration comprend plusieurs activités illustrant les différents usages que pourra accueillir Jemna Connect, notamment un atelier animé par Nefzawa City autour de l’accompagnement des jeunes et de la transformation des idées en projets, ainsi qu’une expérience interactive autour du dessin et de l’intelligence artificielle. Des échanges entre les jeunes et les représentants des missions diplomatiques invités sont également prévus, ainsi qu’un espace podcast intitulé «La voix des jeunes de Jemna» , permettant aux jeunes de partager leurs expériences, leurs projets, leurs idées et leur vision de l’avenir de leur territoire. La cérémonie sera également marquée par l’organisation du «Village des initiatives locales» , mettant à l’honneur les jeunes artisanes de Jemna, les produits du terroir, les savoir-faire locaux ainsi que les initiatives et microprojets soutenus et financés dans le cadre du projet Fe3il.a. La journée sera enfin marquée par la signature officielle du protocole de passation, qui encadre la gestion et l’animation de l’espace et contribue à assurer sa pérennité, avec l’ambition d’en faire un lieu durable de rencontre, d’apprentissage, de collaboration et d’initiative au service des jeunes de Jemna et de la région. Ce projet s’inscrit dans le cadre du programme EU4Youth, à travers le projet «Fe3il.a – Politique jeunesse et participation des jeunes aux politiques publiques en Tunisie» , mis en œuvre par CILG-VNG International, avec le financement de la Délégation de l’Union européenne en Tunisie (DUE) et l’appui de VNG International, l’agence de coopération internationale de l’Association des communes néerlandaises. L’article Jemna Connect, un espace de coworking dédié aux jeunes est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Abidjan : l’ancien Premier ministre guinéen sera inhumé le 9 octobre (proche)
items.description: L’ancien Premier ministre guinéen Sidya Touré, décédé le 25 septembre dernier à Paris des suites d’une maladie, sera inhumé le 9 octobre prochain à Abidjan, en Côte d’Ivoire. L’information a été confirmée à Mediaguinee par l’ancien maire de N’zérékoré, Cécé Loua. Président de l’Union des forces républicaines (UFR), parti dissous, et ancien haut représentant du président Alpha Condé, Sidya Touré s’est éteint à Paris à l’âge de 81 ans. Né en Côte d’Ivoire, où il a notamment été directeur de cabinet du Premier ministre d’alors, Alassane Ouattara, Sidya Touré aura passé de nombreuses années en Guinée, où il comptait de nombreux amis, parmi lesquels l’ancien président de l’Assemblée nationale, Elhadj Aboubacar Somparé. Il avait quitté la Guinée en février 2022 et n’y était plus retourné depuis. Considéré comme un technocrate, Sidya Touré a été une figure majeure de la vie politique guinéenne. Après son départ de la Primature en 1999, il s’est durablement inscrit dans l’opposition, notamment face aux différents régimes qui se sont succédé à la tête du pays. Amara Souza Soumaoro, correspondant régional, N’zérékoré L’article Abidjan : l’ancien Premier ministre guinéen sera inhumé le 9 octobre (proche) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

Irak : les derniers soldats américains quittent le pays
items.description: L'armee americaine acheve son retrait d'Irak, qui doit etre officiellement termine mercredi 30 septembre. Selon un responsable irakien cite par l'agence DPA, les forces americaines de combat et de soutien logistique ont deja quitte le pays, meme si Washington n'avait pas encore confirme la fin complete de l'operation. Ce depart clot la mission de la coalition internationale contre l'organisation etat islamique, selon le calendrier negocie en 2024 entre Washington et Bagdad. Environ 2 500 militaires americains etaient encore presents en Irak ces dernieres annees, principalement dans des fonctions de conseil, de formation et d'appui depuis la fin officielle de leur mission de combat en 2021. Le retrait s'est notamment accelere en septembre depuis les installations du Kurdistan irakien. Retour a la souverainete irakienne Il referme surtout une sequence ouverte il y a 23 ans. Les etats-Unis avaient envahi l'Irak en 2003 et renverse Saddam Hussein, avant de retirer leurs forces en 2011. Ils etaient revenus a partir de 2014 a la demande de Bagdad face a l'expansion de Daesh, qui controlait alors de larges portions du territoire irakien. Pour le gouvernement d' Ali al-Zaïdi , le 30 septembre doit symboliser le retour de la pleine souverainete militaire du pays. Mais le depart americain ouvre une periode delicate. Daesh conserve des cellules clandestines et, surtout, Bagdad doit desormais gerer la question des puissantes factions armees chiites, dont plusieurs entretiennent des liens etroits avec Teheran. Leur desarmement, initialement associe au depart des forces etrangeres, reste inacheve. Le Kurdistan irakien, qui a subi de nombreuses attaques de missiles et de drones, s'inquiete egalement de perdre la protection americaine, notamment les capacites de defense aerienne deployees a Erbil. Le retrait ne signifie toutefois pas la fin des relations entre Washington et Bagdad : une cooperation antiterroriste et securitaire doit se poursuivre sous de nouvelles formes.

items.title: Fiscalité locale : Bafoussam ouvre la Master Class des USFL
items.description: © DR La Commune de Bafoussam III a abrité le 28 septembre 2026 la première journée de la Master Class dédiée au management des Unités de Suivi de la Fiscalité Locale. Plus d'une vingtaine de Collectivités Territoriales Décentralisées de l'Ouest et du Littoral y participent, sous le thème « Manager une USFL : Méthodes, Techniques et Outils », à l'initiative de la NASLA. La mobilisation des ressources propres en ligne de mire. Bafoussam a donné le ton. Le 28 septembre 2026, la Commune de Bafoussam III a accueilli la première étape de la Master Class sur le management des Unités de Suivi de la Fiscalité Locale (USFL), réunissant responsables régionaux et communaux issus de plus d'une vingtaine de CTD des Régions de l'Ouest et du Littoral. Placée sous le thème « Manager une Unité de Suivi de la Fiscalité Locale : Méthodes, Techniques et Outils », la session vise à consolider les compétences des acteurs chargés du suivi fiscal afin d'optimiser l'assiette et les recettes, tout en renforçant la collaboration entre les USFL et les Centres Fiscaux Locaux de Proximité (CFLP). La première journée a été marquée par la présence effective du Directeur Général de la NASLA, qui a personnellement supervisé les travaux, témoignant de l'importance accordée à la mobilisation des ressources propres des collectivités. Au cœur des échanges : les fondamentaux de la fiscalité locale, la planification et l'organisation d'une USFL, le pilotage fiscal et l'élaboration d'un tableau de bord. Les participants ont bénéficié de l'expertise de professionnels de la fiscalité, de la comptabilité budgétaire, du suivi des ressources et des systèmes d'information. À l'issue de cette journée, les participants ont salué la pertinence des enseignements et des outils proposés pour améliorer le suivi fiscal et éclairer la prise de décision. La seconde journée approfondira le management et le leadership d'une USFL, la digitalisation, la gestion des risques, le reporting et l'élaboration d'une feuille de route. Prochaines étapes : Yaoundé les 7-8 octobre, Maroua les 13-14, Bertoua les 19-20 et Buea les 28-29 octobre 2026. Cet article Fiscalité locale : Bafoussam ouvre la Master Class des USFL est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Belgique : nouvelles révélations sur le chat Robert menacé d’expulsion vers l’Algérie
items.description: Le cas du chat menacé d'expulsion vers l’Algérie ou d’euthanasie est devenu une affaire d’opinion publique en Belgique. Une pétition est lancée sur mypetition.org . Elle a déjà obtenu 12366 signatures. Ses initiateurs demandent aux autorités belges d’annuler immédiatement l'ordre de saisie, de placement forcé et d'euthanasie du chaton de six mois et demi. Le chat a été acheté par sa propriétaire sur Internet. Plus tard, un vétérinaire a constaté que le chat, ramené d'Algérie, n’avait pas de “ passeport européen ” et n’était pas vacciné contre la rage. « Contrairement aux fausses informations diffusées de manière irresponsable par la presse belge, la propriétaire ne vient pas de Mons et n'est jamais allée chercher ce chat en Algérie », affirment les auteurs de la pétition. Il a aussitôt saisi l’AFSCA, qui est l’agence belge de sécurité de la chaîne alimentaire. Celle-ci a laissé trois alternatives à la propriétaire : placer le chat en confinement contre 25 euros par jour, l’euthanasier ou le renvoyer en Algérie. Une insistance qui frise l’obsession Les initiateurs de la pétition font état d’un comportement des autorités sanitaires belges qui frise l'obsession. Ils précisent que la propriétaire a fait régulariser Robert à ses frais en août 2026. Le chat possède désormais un passeport européen belge, sa puce électronique a été officiellement remise en ordre et enregistrée, et il a été valablement vacciné contre la rage. De plus, la propriétaire a respecté à la lettre les règles du confinement à domicile qui dure depuis 140 jours, avec un suivi médical régulier. Les arguments de l’administration ne tiennent pas. L’AFSCA justifie son acharnement par la peur théorique de la rage. Or, lit-on dans la pétition, “ scientifiquement, si Robert avait été contaminé à sa naissance, il serait mort depuis des mois ”. Une preuve scientifique apportée, en vain Aussi, une “ preuve scientifique indiscutable ” est apportée par les analyses de sang effectuées par un laboratoire indépendant : “ Le chat est officiellement certifié sain et affiche un taux d'anticorps protecteurs exceptionnel supérieur à 10 UI/mL, soit plus de 20 fois le minimum requis par la loi européenne ”. Ce qui ne fait pas reculer l’administration qui insiste pour que le chat passe par le confinement dans un centre spécialisé, faute de quoi il serait euthanasié ou renvoyé en Algérie. Pour le confinement, il est exigé de la propriétaire une somme qu'elle n’a pas : 25 euros par jour payables d'avance, assortis d'une clause d'indemnité forfaitaire de 5 000 euros en cas de défaut de paiement. L’article Belgique : nouvelles révélations sur le chat Robert menacé d’expulsion vers l’Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Surveillance du plan d’eau : les Douanes et la Marine nationale mutualisent à Douala
items.description: © DR En droite ligne des instructions du directeur général des Douanes, une réunion de coordination s'est tenue le 28 septembre 2026 à la Base navale de Douala entre la Zone I de l'opération HALCOMI IV et le commandement naval, pour définir une surveillance optimale du plan d'eau de la capitale économique. Le front maritime se renforce contre les trafics illicites. Une importante réunion de coordination s'est tenue à la Base Navale de Douala le lundi 28 septembre 2026, en droite ligne des instructions du Directeur Général des Douanes visant à intensifier la lutte contre les trafics illicites. Le Coordonnateur de la Zone I de l'Opération HALCOMI IV, Elvis Manga, était accompagné du Chef des Opérations, le Capitaine Lawin Meka, et de l'Officier de Liaison Marine, le Capitaine Ardant Epoh Mbappe. L'objectif : définir avec le Commandant de la Base Navale de Douala les contours d'une surveillance optimale du plan d'eau. Se félicitant de cette main tendue, le Commandant de la Base et son État-Major ont manifesté leur totale disponibilité, avec un soutien logistique et tactique sans faille, dans l'esprit de la Convention MINFI-MINDEF signée le 11 août 2015 à Yaoundé. Cet accord historique vise à lever les obstacles au déploiement des douaniers sur les espaces maritimes, fluviaux et lacustres, pour renforcer la sécurité nationale, lutter contre la contrebande, la fraude et le crime organisé, et protéger l'espace économique maritime. Cap désormais sur le Sud-Ouest, avec des séances prévues avec la Base Navale de Limbé, la Compagnie Spéciale de Protection de la Sonara et la COPALCO. L'étau se resserre autour des fraudeurs. Cet article Surveillance du plan d'eau : les Douanes et la Marine nationale mutualisent à Douala est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: BEAC : statu quo monétaire malgré le ralentissement de la croissance en zone CEMAC
items.description: © DR Réuni le 28 septembre 2026 à Yaoundé sous la présidence d'Yvon Sana Bangui, le Comité de Politique Monétaire de la BEAC a maintenu ses taux directeurs inchangés : TIAO à 4,50%, facilité de prêt marginal à 5,75%, facilité de dépôt à 0,00% et réserves obligatoires à 6,50% à vue et 4,00% à terme. Prudence et stabilité pour la CEMAC. Le Comité de Politique Monétaire (CPM) de la Banque des Etats de l'Afrique Centrale (BEAC) a tenu sa troisième session ordinaire de l'année, le lundi 28 septembre 2026 à Yaoundé, sous la présidence de Monsieur Yvon SANA BANGUI, Gouverneur de la BEAC. Au cours de cette session, le CPM a examiné les perspectives macroéconomiques internationales et sous-régionales, ainsi que la situation du système financier de la CEMAC. Au niveau international, le FMI prévoit, selon sa mise à jour de juillet 2026, une croissance mondiale qui reviendrait à 3,0% en 2026 contre 3,5% en 2025, en raison des tensions géopolitiques. Au niveau de la CEMAC, les prévisions de la BEAC tablent sur un ralentissement : croissance à 3,0% contre 3,7% en 2025, inflation contenue sous la norme communautaire à 2,2% contre 2,0%, repli du déficit budgétaire hors dons de 4,5% à 3,3% du PIB, et amélioration du déficit courant à 2,8% contre 4,2%. La masse monétaire progresserait de 10,6%, les réserves de change passeraient à 4,53 mois d'importations contre 4,07 mois, et le taux de couverture extérieure s'établirait à 72,4% contre 65,2% en 2025. En définitive, le CPM a décidé le statu quo monétaire pour accompagner la résilience tout en préservant la stabilité. Cet article BEAC : statu quo monétaire malgré le ralentissement de la croissance en zone CEMAC est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Sonatel s’associe à Saly Sarr pour accompagner son ascension sportive
items.description: Sonatel a officialisé, lundi à Dakar, un partenariat avec la triple-sauteuse sénégalaise Saly Sarr. Cette convention vise à soutenir la championne dans la poursuite de sa carrière et à contribuer à l’émergence de nouveaux talents sportifs. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence de la ministre de la Jeunesse et des Sports. Pour Saly Sarr, cet accord intervient au terme d’une saison exceptionnelle, marquée par plusieurs performances de premier plan sur la scène internationale. Le 23 août, elle a remporté le meeting de Diamond League de Silésie, en Pologne, avec un bond de 15,08 m, établissant un nouveau record national. Le 4 septembre, elle a ensuite décroché la finale de la Diamond League à Bruxelles, avec 14,96 m, devenant la première athlète sénégalaise à remporter ce circuit. Elle a prolongé cette dynamique en s’imposant au World Athletics Ultimate Championship, à Budapest, le 13 septembre, avec un saut de 15,06 m. La championne a exprimé sa reconnaissance à Sonatel, estimant que ce soutien constitue à la fois une marque de confiance et une responsabilité supplémentaire. Elle entend poursuivre sa progression, relever de nouveaux défis et continuer à porter les couleurs du Sénégal. Son parcours doit également, selon elle, encourager les jeunes, notamment les filles, à croire en leurs capacités et à s’investir dans le sport. Le directeur général de Sonatel Brelotte Bâ, a salué les performances de l’athlète, mettant en avant sa discipline, son travail et sa persévérance. Il a rappelé que l’entreprise accompagne le sport sénégalais depuis plus de 25 ans, à travers des partenariats avec des fédérations et des sportifs. Le groupe souhaite aussi faire de cette convention un levier de détection et d’accompagnement de jeunes talents. Présente à la cérémonie, la ministre de la Jeunesse et des Sports a salué une initiative qui illustre, selon elle, la nécessité de renforcer les liens entre les champions et le secteur privé. Elle a rappelé que le ministère entend faciliter ces passerelles afin d’offrir aux sportifs de meilleures conditions d’évolution. Elle a également appelé d’autres entreprises à s’engager en faveur de la jeunesse et du sport. À travers cet accord, Sonatel entend ainsi prolonger son accompagnement du sport national, tandis que Saly Sarr bénéficie d’un nouveau soutien pour poursuivre son parcours au plus haut niveau. C.G.D
