items.title: Pacte national de stabilité sociale : le Comité de pilotage convoqué le 15 octobre par le Premier ministre
items.description: Le suivi des engagements pris dans le cadre du Pacte national de stabilité sociale pour une croissance inclusive et durable (PNSS-CID) sera au cœur d’une réunion du Comité de pilotage prévue le jeudi 15 octobre 2026, sous la présidence du Premier ministre. L’annonce a été faite par le ministre de la Fonction publique, du Travail et de la Réforme du service public, Mamadou Lamnine Diante, lors du symposium social organisé par le Conseil national du patronat (CNP). Cette rencontre, placée sous le thème « Investissement privé, Gouvernance d’entreprise, Liberté syndicale, Dialogue social et Paix sociale : quelles responsabilités des Employeurs, des Travailleurs et de l’État ? », doit permettre de faire le point sur la mise en œuvre des engagements contenus dans le Pacte. Selon Mamadou Lamnine Diante, le Premier ministre a été informé de l’état d’exécution de ces engagements dès les premières séances de travail organisées après sa prise de fonction. À cette occasion, il lui a été rappelé que le chef du Gouvernement, en sa qualité de président du Comité de pilotage, est tenu de rencontrer les organisations d’employeurs et de travailleurs une fois par an. Le Premier ministre a toutefois exprimé sa volonté de renforcer la fréquence de ces échanges. Il a fait savoir qu’il n’entendait pas attendre une année entière avant de rencontrer les partenaires sociaux et s’est déclaré favorable à la tenue de réunions trimestrielles du Comité de pilotage. C’est dans cette perspective qu’il a demandé la convocation rapide de l’instance, dont la prochaine session est fixée au 15 octobre. Le ministre a également annoncé que les organisations patronales et syndicales recevront prochainement leurs convocations, accompagnées du document préparatoire de la réunion, actuellement en cours d’élaboration. À travers le PNSS-CID, le Gouvernement entend s’appuyer sur un cadre de concertation fondé sur des engagements réciproques entre les différentes parties. Ceux-ci doivent faire l’objet d’un suivi régulier, d’une évaluation collective et, au besoin, d’ajustements convenus entre les acteurs concernés. C.G.D

items.title: Inside the Biggest Feud in Artificial Intelligence
items.description: Being in San Francisco in the mid-2020s sometimes feels like what I imagine living in Los Alamos was like in 1943, when the Manhattan Project rolled into town. The air is heavy with excitement and dread. Engineers toil, day and night, on systems of profound consequence. Wild-eyed prophets sell visions of a transformed world, and politicians drop in to check on the progress of the project. ­Everyone knows that the fates of nations, and trillions of dollars of capital, rely on what happens here, yet no one can fully appreciate what it would mean if the project succeeds. One person consumed by this question is Dario Amodei , a Princeton-educated physicist who in 2016 left Google to join OpenAI, then a fledgling nonprofit AI research lab. He looked the part of a mad scientist, with round glasses and short brown ringlets that he twisted in his fingers whenever he was feeling nervous or thinking hard about something. He was known among his colleagues as a brilliant, bullheaded researcher with deep convictions about AI, which he often expressed by writing long essays that he circulated inside the company. The most famous of these essays among OpenAI workers was a 26-page document titled “Big Blob of Compute.” Amodei wrote it in 2017, shortly after arriving at OpenAI, and it spelled out his grand theory of intelligence—how it emerged in nature, how it could be built into AI systems, and how it could be developed safely. Amodei’s hypothesis that machine intelligence was primarily a function of scale—that AI systems got smarter as they got bigger—steered OpenAI’s research agenda toward large language models, which Amodei saw as a promising path to artificial general intelligence, or AGI, a human-level intelligence capable of doing anything the brain can. By the middle of 2020, three teams were racing toward AGI: OpenAI, DeepMind, and Google Brain. But a fourth team was quietly assembling under Amodei, then OpenAI’s vice president of research. Amodei and his team had led the development of GPT-­2, then GPT-­3, and he was feeling ever more certain that he wasn’t going to stick around for GPT-­4. Career-wise, things were going great for Amodei. GPT-­3 was a hit among programmers, and his research on large language models was starting to bear fruit. A year earlier, two researchers on Amodei’s team, Jared Kaplan and Sam McCandlish, came up with what they called the “scaling laws”—equations that described predictable increases in LLM performance as you poured more data, compute, and parameters into them. Another researcher on his team, Paul Christiano, pioneered a technique called “reinforcement learning from human feedback,” or RLHF, which allowed OpenAI to steer its models away from harmful outputs. A third team under Amodei was already making plans for GPT-4, which would be orders of magnitude bigger than GPT-3. But along the way, Amodei lost faith in the company’s leadership. He had come to believe that Sam Altman was a two-­faced manipulator and that OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, was power-­hungry and reckless. Amodei had qualms about their decision to turn OpenAI into a commercial enterprise, and thought that they were straying from the nonprofit’s original mission to “benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return.” Most of all, he was sick of the tribal warfare that had turned the whole place into a viper’s nest and forced him to fight for ideas he thought should be obvious. One person who spoke to Amodei during this time said that Amodei considered OpenAI “a shit show” that was “run by low-­integrity people.” If he hadn’t reached his breaking point yet, it seemed possible that he soon would. “Every day there was a new crisis, a new crazy thing that Sam was about to do in 24 hours if Dario didn’t throw an absolute temper tantrum,” the person said. That year, Amodei started pulling members of his team aside to tell them about all the objectionable things he’d seen. The worst, in his opinion, was a fundraising scheme that Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever, two of OpenAI’s co-founders, had cooked up back in 2017, when Elon Musk was pulling away from Open­AI and the company needed a new source of funding. Their idea, which ­became known as the “countries plan,” was to set up an auction between governments, including the United States, China, and Russia, for the rights to OpenAI’s future AGI technology, according to five people familiar with the plan. The plan had started months earlier, as a more benign proposal to explore the idea of creating an international coalition to promote the benefits and manage the risks of AGI. But by the time Brockman and Sutskever pitched the plan to OpenAI employees at an internal presentation that winter, it had turned into a fundraising strategy. Brockman and Sutskever rationalized the plan by claiming that AGI—­if and when it arrived—­would have such powerful national-security implications that governments would seize it from the private companies that developed it, according to two people familiar with their thinking. And if OpenAI might be forced to hand over AGI to Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia eventually, why not sell it to them now, when the company needed the money? “It sounded like tech people pitching an insane start-up, where they have this wacky plan and then at the end of the plan, it’s like, We’ll make the government pay for it ,” one person who heard the presentation told me. (An OpenAI spokesperson insisted to me that although the company “briefly considered whether to turn OpenAI into an international cooperative endeavor,” it “did not consider selling AGI to China or Russia.”) Amodei was horrified when he heard about the countries plan. Were they insane? Selling AGI to dictators, he believed, was the exact opposite of OpenAI’s mission, and it was a slap in the face to people including the members of his safety team, who joined OpenAI because they believed it was a noble cause. In December 2017, he wrote an email to Brockman and Sutskever, along with some other top OpenAI executives, spelling out his objections to the countries plan. He wrote that the original idea of an international AGI coalition “seems to have morphed over the course of a couple weeks into something I strongly believe is a bad idea: a plan to sell AGI to governments, e.g. Russia, China, and the US; or raise money from those countries with a promise to do so; or perhaps even play countries off against each other in an attempt to get funding.” He continued: “In my opinion this plan would exacerbate rather than reduce arms races, would potentially enable human rights atrocities (giving someone like the Russian government ‘an AGI that implements their values’ would allow them to do unspeakably awful things to their people), and would undermine OpenAI’s moral legitimacy.” Instead, Amodei said, OpenAI should be optimizing for what is “good for humanity.” His protests turned out to be moot. After Musk pulled out, the company found new funding from Microsoft and abandoned the countries plan. But Amodei never forgot how seriously Brockman and Sutskever had considered an idea he found morally obscene. In 2018 and 2019, Amodei objected to a number of other business decisions OpenAI made, such as selling access to GPT-­3 through an API. But his biggest concern was about Altman’s character. He recorded examples of times he felt Altman had misled him. During private beta-testing for GPT-­3, for instance, he’d asked Altman for a list of the customers who had been approved to use GPT-­3. Altman sent him one. But Amodei claimed that he had discovered another, longer list of approved customers, which Altman hadn’t told him about. Amodei also thought he’d caught Altman misrepresenting his negotiations with Microsoft for a new, $1 billion investment; Altman told Amodei that Microsoft had rejected certain safety-related provisions of the deal that Amodei had wanted to include. One of these provisions was about OpenAI’s so-­called merge-and-assist clause—­a line in OpenAI’s charter, which Amodei had written, that committed OpenAI to stop competing with, and start assisting with, any “value-aligned, safety-­conscious” project that “comes close to building AGI before we do.” During the Microsoft negotiations, Amodei had insisted that Microsoft shouldn’t be able to veto an acquisition of OpenAI—­the most likely way that a merge-and-assist would be enacted—­but Altman had told him that Microsoft wouldn’t agree to the term. Amodei believed that Altman had been so ­eager to get the deal done that he conceded the provision ­(or never asked for it in the first place), then lied to him about it. Some of their disputes were related to business and strategy decisions, but others seemed more like ethical lapses to Amodei. Altman, for example, had met Kanye West and offered to let him into the GPT-­3 private beta in 2020, according to two people familiar with the offer. Jack Clark, OpenAI’s policy director, quashed the idea, pointing out that West had recently posted a video that seemed to show himself urinating on a Grammy award and appeared to be mentally unstable. (This was before the period in which West began to publicly express admiration for Hitler.) There were many more examples on Amodei’s list—­times he thought Altman had acted recklessly, or seemed to get caught in a lie. Few of them were worth quitting over, on their own. But they added up to a picture of a person who, in Amodei’s mind, couldn’t be trusted with a technology as powerful as AGI. His sister, Daniela Amodei, was also getting fed up with OpenAI. She and Brockman had once been close. (Brockman even gave a toast at her 2017 wedding to Holden Karnofsky, who joined OpenAI’s nonprofit board that year.) But years of working together had strained their relationship. She had also started to clash with Mira Murati, then OpenAI’s vice president of applied AI and partnerships, over who was in charge of making decisions related to safety. Inside OpenAI, some employees viewed Daniela as her brother’s high-­EQ counterpart. She was a skilled manager who had majored in English literature in college and worked in politics before her career in tech. But as her role expanded to include managing more of OpenAI’s technical teams, she collided with Brockman and other leaders, who came to see her as the third member of an inflexible triumvirate that included Dario and Karnofsky. Daniela had an unusual process for working through conflicts. She and Karnofsky had a large collection of stuffed animals, which they treated as their personal advisory council for managerial role-playing. Each animal had an assigned character profile. Jinji was a lazy cat who encouraged Daniela to cancel meetings and avoid taking on too much work. Maura, a pink bear, was a detail-­oriented, type-­A manager. A panda named Beary Bonds was the “patron bear of generosity and empathy.” She treated these exercises as something between an inside joke and an earnest management technique. (In 2023, she told me the animals were “very useful in analyzing different personality types.”) And although not many people at OpenAI knew about the animals, the ones who did weren’t sure how seriously she took their advice. That year, the Amodeis began building their own nucleus inside Open­ AI. “Dario’s clique,” as some people called it—­though it was really both his and Daniela’s—­set up private Slack channels and held their own meetings. They talked constantly about safety, using jargon that was unfamiliar to the more technical engineers. And to the people who weren’t invited, it felt standoffish—­a safety splinter cell that was refusing to work with anyone else. “Dario had a habit at the time of just saying, We must do X; it is the morally correct thing to do. It was like a shortcut to win any argument—­‘because safety.’ And that really pissed the non-­safety teams off,” one former colleague told me. Amodei had considered quitting before, but he’d always talked himself out of it. Staying and fighting for OpenAI’s mission, he reasoned, was better than letting other, less safety-­minded people do the job. He knew that OpenAI had the most talented researchers in the industry, and the best chance of getting to AGI, and he thought that he could change the company from the inside. But one day in 2019, he emailed his housemates, and a few close colleagues on the safety team, and told them that he had given up on making OpenAI work. Any progress that the safety team made was bound to be temporary, he said, and would always be overridden by Altman and Brockman’s commercial priorities. He thought about going to work for DeepMind, whose safety work he respected. But Jared Kaplan, the physics professor who led scaling-laws research at OpenAI, suggested a different idea: What if Amodei gathered all the people at the company who shared his views on safety, and they started their own company together? Amodei was initially skeptical. Did the world need one more company racing toward AGI? Wouldn’t a mass exodus of safety-­minded OpenAI employees make the company even more dangerous? But the more he thought about Kaplan’s idea, the more he liked it. In 2020, the year GPT-3 came out, Amodei approached a few members of his clique and pitched them on the idea of leaving OpenAI together to start a new company. Like OpenAI, the new company would do cutting-­edge AI research focused on scaling up large language models. But they would be surrounded by other people who cared deeply about safety, and they would be free of OpenAI’s constant drama and infighting. Within a few weeks, Amodei had collected seven co-founders: himself, Daniela, Jack Clark, Sam McCandlish, Tom Brown, Chris Olah, and Jared Kaplan. (An eighth co-founder, Ben Mann, was added later.) That was enough to get started. And once they told the rest of OpenAI that they were leaving, more would certainly follow. Amodei didn’t want to leave right away. First, he decided to tell Altman about his plans and offer him a list of conditions under which he’d agree to stay. He suspected those conditions—­which would include giving the safety team veto power over new product releases—­probably wouldn’t fly. But Amodei hoped that the threat of leaving, and bringing some of OpenAI’s brightest minds with him, would force Altman to take them seriously. While Amodei negotiated with Altman, the group of seven formed a private Slack channel and called it BATNA, which stood for “best alternative to a negotiated agreement,” a wonky business-­school term that referred to their option of walking away. And they started to plan their escape. Once it became clear that Altman wasn’t going to give Amodei what he wanted, the BATNA group hired a lawyer and began negotiating the terms of what they started calling “the divorce.” Altman agreed that the BATNA group could poach any other Open­AI employees it wanted for a period of several weeks, in exchange for agreeing not to poach any more for a year afterward. Daniela Amodei, who was leading the negotiations on the BATNA group’s side, asked to take some of their internal research documents with them to the new company. They agreed to sign a mutual non-disparagement agreement, each group pledging that it wouldn’t bad-mouth the other in public. Then, in December 2020, OpenAI employees got an invitation to an all-­staff virtual meeting. Altman began the meeting as if it were a normal weekly update. He ran through updates on OpenAI’s research and announced a few new hires. Then he turned the floor over to Amodei, who announced that he and six other OpenAI leaders were quitting to start their own, safety-­focused AI organization. Emoji, exclamation points, and shocked messages flooded the meeting’s chat window as Amodei put a positive spin on the news. He said that OpenAI would continue to pursue its mission of creating AGI for the benefit of humanity, and he gave only the vaguest details about why the seven employees had decided to leave. A final message, from Jack Clark, appeared in the chat: “I love you all.” Then, suddenly, their screens went dark. OpenAI had removed them from the call, revoked their email and Slack access, and remotely bricked their laptops. Altman stayed on the call and tried to reassure panicked employees that OpenAI would continue operating as normal. But employees were ­already texting one another, trying to figure out what had happened. Some wondered whether anyone would be left to train GPT-­4. Others tried to figure out who their new managers would be, or which of their co-workers were joining the new venture. A few hours later, the newly unemployed co-founders held their own video call—­BATNA’s first meeting. There was plenty of business to attend to, and plenty of unanswered questions to worry about. How could seven people possibly hope to compete with OpenAI and Google? Where would they get the GPUs and the data and the money? Who would handle the boring corporate stuff, like filing the legal paperwork and buying­ everyone new laptops? What would they call themselves? (“Anthropic,” it would turn out, although the company originally planned to call itself “Sparrow Systems,” after a parable from Nick Bostrom’s 2014 book Superintelligence , until the co-founders realized the domain name wasn’t available.) But there would be time to answer those questions later. For now, they celebrated, raising glasses to one another in their virtual meeting boxes, smiling and laughing more than any of them had in months. They didn’t know exactly what to do next, or what the future would hold. But they were free. Five years later, Anthropic—which now has thousands of employees, a high-profile feud with the Pentagon, and a trillion-dollar IPO on the horizon—barely resembles the company Dario Amodei and his colleagues set out to create. Initially, they conceived of themselves as a small AI-safety research lab, not a product company. Anthropic’s founding document, a 2021 Amodei essay titled “Vision for a NewCo,” envisioned a company of roughly 50 employees (to ensure “extreme talent density”) and predicted that building AGI would cost only about $10 billion. When I first visited Anthropic’s headquarters, in the summer of 2023, the entire company consisted of about 160 earnest AI-safety obsessives cooped up together in a Jackson Square office building, a floor above an elder-care organization. Inside, engineers played board games and ate vegan sandwiches before heading back to their desks to hack on the next version of Claude, Anthropic’s chatbot. There were plants everywhere, and hundreds of empty cans of Liquid Death, a trendy sparkling-water brand, that an engineer had fashioned into a towering throne. It looked like a college botany lab, or maybe the headquarters of a prosperous cult. But when I returned in the winter of 2025, the cult had transformed into a command center. Anthropic’s workforce had swelled to thousands of employees, and it had taken over the former headquarters of Slack, in a sleek, industrial high-rise on Howard Street. A dozen brawny security guards stood watch at the entrance. Upstairs, past the guards, the company had turned most of its office space into a high-­security containment zone. Visitors were allowed onto only certain floors, and getting onto some of the other floors—including the one where new versions of Claude were being trained—­required special clearance even for employees. There were still hints of the old Anthropic: a lush arboretum, a library with a copy of The Making of the Atomic Bomb , Amodei’s favorite book, which had once been required reading for new Anthropic employees. But everything else was different. Anthropic had become one of the fastest-growing companies in the history of capitalism, and was running neck and neck with OpenAI in the race to AGI. Amodei and his co-founders had become globe-­trotting tech celebrities, and Amodei—­who had always tried to live below his means, and was slightly embarrassed by his new station—­now traveled to fancy conferences on a charter jet, flanked by a team of bodyguards. The company had turned several of his mega-essays—such as “Machines of Loving Grace,” a 15,000-word paean to AI optimism, and “The Adolescence of Technology,” a gloomier follow-up—into expensively printed books. Upstairs, Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s president, now spend their days managing long lists of what Jack Clark, another Anthropic co-founder, calls “success disasters.” “It’s stressful on every dimension,” Daniela told me. “And it’s scary because we can lose it at any time. That’s just on the business side. Then there’s the mission, and we’re like, Are we accidentally making things worse? Like, we think we have all the safety stuff figured out, but do we? ” One thing that hasn’t changed is the Amodeis’ rivalry with OpenAI. Dario and Daniela still despise Altman and Brockman, according to several people who know them well. And Dario, who is less filtered on Anthropic’s Slack than he is in his public appearances, has written in internal messages that Altman and OpenAI are “evil.” (An executive on Anthropic’s communications team asked him to delete one such message, around the time of the 2023 OpenAI board coup, out of fear that it might leak.) The feud goes both ways. In private, some people at OpenAI have described the Amodeis as power-­hungry virtue-­signalers, not principled humanitarians. OpenAI employees gossip about Anthropic’s connections to effective altruism and accuse the company of hypocrisy, for publicly warning of AI’s risks while privately accelerating the race. And despite the companies’ recent willingness to cooperate on safety measures, few people who know Altman, Brockman, and the Amodeis expect them to make amends anytime soon. Workers at both companies have noted the irony that although their bosses train AI models to be kind and compassionate, they can’t stop trashing one another. For now, it seems, the “machines of loving grace” will be built by humans of bitter spite. This article is adapted from Roose’s book, The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence .

items.title: The THAAD Delusion
items.description: M ohamed bin Zayed was worried about Iran —so worried, in fact, that he decided to gamble with his nation’s future. “We are living in a dangerous neighborhood,” the crown prince of Abu Dhabi and de facto leader of the United Arab Emirates told the top U.S. Air Force general in February 2007. Iran’s effort to acquire nuclear weapons, he said, must be delayed “by all means available.” But MBZ, as the crown prince is known, was acutely aware of what public opposition to the ambitions of its much larger neighbor—and $7 billion trading partner—could cost his tiny state. “I am putting my country at risk and placing myself in a dangerous spot,” he told General Michael Moseley. So he had an urgent request to make of the United States. He wanted a complete multilayered missile shield in place by the summer of 2009, to protect the Emirates against Iranian retribution. American officials could scarcely conceal their glee. MBZ’s request was the payoff of a year-long campaign to enlist the UAE in their effort to curtail Iran’s nuclear program. They understood that unless the Emirates could defend itself against an Iranian missile barrage, this was unlikely to happen. For a decade, the American weapons manufacturer Raytheon had been trying, unsuccessfully, to persuade the Emiratis to invest in its Patriot air-defense system, but UAE officials were skeptical of its efficacy. However, by 2007, the United States had something new to offer—a system so technologically advanced that it didn’t fully exist yet. The dream of an anti-ballistic-missile shield dated back to the Reagan administration’s Strategic Defense Initiative. At the time, the idea of firing one missile to hit another missile mid-flight, like shooting a bullet to hit another bullet, was derided as “Star Wars.” But in the late 1990s, after Star Wars had been quietly abandoned, Lockheed Martin scientists proved that it was actually possible for a bullet to hit a bullet. They dubbed their system Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD. It was designed to be mobile. The final product was a large, rectangular set of launch tubes carried on the back of a snub-nosed military transport truck. The launch tubes could pivot backwards, like the bed of a dump truck, and point the missiles skyward before firing them. It hardly looked high-tech. An Army Theatre High Altitude Area Defense System (THAAD) is displayed on Capitol Hill Wedensday April 29, 1998. (Joe Marquette / AP) Earlier that day in 2007, technicians from Raytheon and Lockheed had explained to MBZ that, in spite of the launcher’s humble appearance, it was the linchpin of a cutting-edge system. The THAAD functioned as part of a network of devices. After space satellites detected a missile launch, giant, land-based radar systems would track the missile in flight. A mobile THAAD battery could aim its interceptors and fire. Then an infrared sensor in the THAAD missile’s nose cone would become its eyes, as an onboard computer adjusted its course in fractions of a second. [ Read: How the U.S. squandered its strategic advantage ] The Pentagon had devised a new system, called the Bilateral Air Defense Initiative, that would employ the THAAD as part of a triple-layered defense, backed up by the Patriot system and short-range air defenses, or SHORAD. These would all be wired to a new early-warning radar system that could spot incoming missiles. The THAAD was at the zenith of this system because it could hit missiles in the upper atmosphere. The Patriot could intercept missiles that got through, hitting them at lower altitudes. The SHORAD could protect troops. U.S. diplomats and military brass did not emphasize that the system had only just been approved for production. The first THAAD missiles would not even be delivered until 2011. But MBZ was sold. It would take only 46 seconds for an Iranian missile to reach the UAE, and the THAAD could protect the country’s oil refineries, skyscrapers, museums, and airports. The Emiratis soon made U.S. missile-defense systems a “top priority” for their military spending, according to State Department cables. “For the Emiratis, Iran is a primordial obsession,” one cable reported in 2009. The UAE would become the first foreign country to buy and deploy the THAAD. In 2022, this bargain proved its worth when a THAAD interceptor knocked down Houthi missiles aimed at the UAE. By that time, Saudi Arabia had also purchased the THAAD, in 2017. Two years later, in 2019, Israel participated in a THAAD training exercise, and it was lent a U.S. THAAD battery in 2023. By early 2026, the THAAD was the umbrella that protected U.S. interests and allies across the Middle East. It seemed to promise security. But the war with Iran has exposed the flaw in this scheme. The THAAD was never designed to protect an entire country. As capable as the system might be, it was created with a narrow mission in mind: to protect U.S. troops in combat for an extremely limited time. The Army, which oversaw air-defense systems like the THAAD, had wanted a system that could fend off an initial wave of missile attacks long enough for U.S. fighter jets and naval destroyers to fully respond. “What you needed to do was just survive the first salvo, right? Protect your high-value military deployments, the ports, right from the initial salvo, and then we just go destroy them, and the war’s over,” John Ferrari, a retired Army major general who supervised the THAAD system when he was the commander of the White Sands Missile Range, told me. In the war with Iran, the THAAD has worked precisely as designed—but not at all as promised. The system performed well in the early days of the conflict, intercepting Iranian ballistic missiles with impressive accuracy. But the U.S. has not destroyed many of Iran’s missile launchers, and the war is far from over. And despite planning for just such a conflict for two decades, the U.S. failed to take the steps necessary to convert the THAAD into a system that could provide protection for as long as it would be relied upon to do so. The U.S. neither amassed a stockpile of THAAD interceptors large enough to see it through a war, nor figured out how to build new ones fast enough to replace them as they are fired. Those are hardly unique failures. Throughout the U.S. military, as the war with Iran grinds on, exquisitely engineered systems are running out of the munitions necessary to make them work. But nowhere are those failures more stark, or more consequential, than with the THAAD. I n 2024, after nearly 20 years of procurement , the United States had a stockpile of no more than 534 THAAD interceptor missiles, according to Pentagon documents. The Emiratis had somewhere between 190 and 290 THAAD missiles, according to arms-sales notifications and Pentagon records. The Saudis, who had just gotten their first THAAD battery up and running, had a stockpile of unknown size. These stockpiles turned out to be a precious national resource for all three countries. Over the past year, though, the stockpiles have been rapidly spent down. The munitions spending began in earnest last summer, when Israel and the United States struck Iran, eliciting a wave of missile attacks that triggered the interceptors. The spending accelerated this year, when both countries attacked Iran in force and unleashed a munitions-draining war. During 10 months of conflict in the Middle East, the United States burned through a stockpile of THAAD missiles that took roughly nine years to build. Nearly 80 percent of that stockpile is gone, according to recent estimates by CNN. The drawdown has led to a scramble. The Army has rotated THAADs out of South Korea to backfill supplies in the Middle East, while the Pentagon hopes to invest billions of dollars in a race to produce more THAAD missiles—a project that will be finished in 2030 in the best-case scenario. Munitions stockpiles have long been a neglected element of U.S. military strategy. Pentagon budget writers favor flashier line items, such as new fighter jets and naval destroyers. And munitions procurement relies on a fragile U.S. industrial base that is plagued by points of failure. They are produced by large U.S. defense contractors—such as Lockheed Martin, which makes the THAAD—whose business models constrain them from ramping up production even when a missile shortage is evident. The THAAD-missile deficit is part of a larger emergency, reflecting patterns that cut across the U.S. munitions supply. The United States and its allies have also burned through supplies of Patriot interceptors, which are often fired in concert with the THAAD. The Tomahawk, an offensive missile, has been used at such a rate that prewar stockpiles won’t be replenished for another four years, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Stockpiles of other offensive missiles, with names like JASSM and PrSM, have been drained to levels that will take months to replenish. [ Read: The one variable that could decide the war ] The missile depletion has reverberated throughout America’s network of military alliances. The point of many arms sales, former Assistant Secretary of State John Hillen told me, is to bind the militaries of U.S. allies with U.S. forces. “Part of our diplomatic framework was to ensure better cooperation in real-time situations,” said Hillen, who played a key role in selling the UAE on the THAAD. “It’s helpful for people to have the same kit, as the Brits would say.” By selling the THAAD and other systems interoperable with those used by the American military to key allies, the U.S. hoped to bring them more closely into the American orbit. But countries that joined the club are now finding that their membership doesn’t guarantee speedy access to U.S. missiles. Switzerland ordered a suite of Patriot interceptors after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, but was recently told to expect a four-to-five-year delay . The Swiss are now looking for other suppliers. The Polish military recently refused a U.S. request to send its interceptor missiles to the Middle East to backfill supplies. Denmark abandoned an $8.5 billion order for Patriots after deciding to prioritize the speed of acquisition, choosing a different system made in Europe. Soon after the U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury in February against Iran, Saudi Arabia announced a new security pact with Ukraine to access Kyiv’s cheaper anti-drone weapons. Many of America’s allies are now looking for a Plan B. E ach THAAD interceptor is essentially assembled by hand, piece by piece, at a Lockheed Martin production facility in Troy, Alabama. Lockheed declined to offer a tour of the plant, citing national-security concerns, but photographs from inside the factory show why production is so time-consuming and expensive. Rows of partially assembled missiles line the floor, their half-open interiors exposing a maze of tubes, circuits, wires, and sensors. Employees sit on wheeled chairs alongside the missiles and painstakingly connect new components. If one connection is faulty, or one circuit board is bad, the result is worse than useless—an interceptor that misses isn’t just a waste, but a squandered opportunity to save lives. Each missile costs about $12 million. As intricate as the assembly might be, Lockheed’s factory in Troy is actually one of the simpler parts of the THAAD production chain. The industrial base behind the THAAD traces back to hundreds of suppliers that provide microchips, infrared sensors, rocket motors, and specialized fuel propellant. Building this industrial ecosystem was almost as complicated as inventing a missile that could hit a missile; the complexity hindered THAAD production for many years. In 2016, for example, a third-party supplier changed its manufacturing process for a connector that went into the THAAD without telling Lockheed Martin. This caused problems that shut down THAAD production for months. To complicate matters further, the THAAD was born within the kind of bureaucratic labyrinth that only the Pentagon seems capable of creating. The missile itself was developed and purchased by a Pentagon branch created to accelerate high-tech missile innovation, renamed the Missile Defense Agency in 2002 by the George W. Bush administration. But once the agency designed and purchased the THAAD interceptors, it handed them over to the Army to operate. This built an unresolved tension into the THAAD system from the beginning, in ways that limited the stockpile: The Missile Defense Agency was used to operating with a large budget; the Army was in the habit of pinching pennies. Major General Ferrari, who oversaw THAAD procurement for the Army, told me the Army resisted pouring money into the THAAD program because of its cost. He bristled when the MDA presented the Army with the bill for new THAADs. “You’re like: Dude, you know, I’m over here eating at McDonald’s, and you’re there at the three-star Michelin restaurant, right? Like, I can’t afford this, right? And that was the tension,” Ferrari said. The Army has struggled ever since to shoulder the THAAD’s high cost. Maintenance work on a THAAD battery deployed in Guam was conducted under a tarp rather than a proper hangar, according to a Government Accountability Office report. The purchase of interceptor missiles was also hindered over the years by the THAAD’s underlying strategic mission that it would be needed only to protect against the first salvo. This short-term use didn’t justify keeping an enormous supply of expensive missiles in reserve. The first-salvo concept was baked into THAAD purchasing when the Pentagon set the missile’s Acquisition Program Baseline, even as the THAAD was being promoted as the keystone piece of homeland-defense shields for foreign countries. Program baselines can be revisited over the years, but they tend to acquire a persistent inertia that carries forward. This image provided by the U.S. Air Force shows the U.S. Army Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) launching station preparing to load onto a 4th Airlift Squadron C-17 Globemaster III at Fort Bliss, Texas, Feb. 23, 2019. (Staff Sgt. Cory D. Payne / U.S. Air Force / AP) The THAAD purchases were further constrained after 2011, when Congress and the Obama White House were at loggerheads over the budget. Congress had devised a budget-cutting plan, called “sequestration,” that was supposed to be a radical bargaining tool, imposing Pentagon spending cuts that the White House found unacceptable. But the negotiations failed, and sequestration arrived. Frank Kendall oversaw weapons procurement at the Pentagon during the period of sequestration. He spent several months of every year engaged in contentious horse-trading sessions among military branches and various offices under the secretary of defense that were fighting for money within the annual budget. Each military branch submitted its ideal budget in June. Every service had a wish list, but there was never enough money to go around. The service branches tended to fight for their premier-weapons systems, such as fighter jets, tanks, and destroyers. In the best-case scenario, missile stockpiles were treated as a lower priority. More often, they were treated as the best budget line to slash in order to afford pricier platforms. It was easy to dial up or dial down the number of missiles purchased in a given year, making them a ripe target for cuts. “You can slice it a little bit. It’s like salami slicing, right? You trim a little bit off, get a little bit of money,” Kendall told me. “Munitions tend to be things that people won’t fight for as much.” The U.S. THAAD stockpile was built in a slow drip over many years. By 2014, the United States had 48 THAAD interceptors, according to Pentagon procurement documents. In the 2015 fiscal year, only three THAAD missiles were delivered to the MDA. The following year, another 43 missiles were delivered. By 2022, the United States had built a stockpile of roughly 460 THAAD interceptors, according to procurement documents that outlined how many interceptors had actually been delivered (573 had been ordered). In February of that year, Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine. T he flow of missiles to Ukraine began in earnest in late 2021, when U.S. intelligence agencies sensed that Putin might be gathering his forces for an invasion. In the years that followed, the United States sent Javelin missiles, Patriot interceptors, TOW missiles, Stinger missiles, and other munitions to the country. The THAAD was never given to the Ukrainians, but the war would draw down stockpiles of Patriot interceptors, which are an integral part of the same multilayered defensive shield. The Biden administration orchestrated the movement of missiles to Ukraine using a novel technique called the Presidential Drawdown Authority, an obscure arms-transfer law enacted in the 1960s. The PDA system was initially designed to shift small amounts of equipment from the U.S. to its allies, and was capped at transferring about $100 million worth of materiel each year. In 2022, Congress raised that cap to $11 billion, and then raised it again to $14.5 billion the following year. [ Read: Ukraine may be just the ally America needs ] The PDA was an imperfect vehicle for massive arms transfers. The system didn’t contain a formal mechanism to ensure that U.S. missile stockpiles were replenished at the same rate that they were being drawn down. The Pentagon hastily created a new committee to oversee arms shipments to Ukraine, called the Cross Department Working Group. When the Government Accountability Office asked the Pentagon to provide the formal guidelines for the missile shipments to Ukraine, instead of furnishing a detailed policy paper, the undersecretary of defense for policy provided a set of four slides. By September 2023, Pentagon officials were concerned about the rate at which U.S. stockpiles were being depleted. The Cross Department Working Group adopted a new policy that month, requiring Pentagon planners to consider whether Congress had provided enough money to refill stockpiles before new shipments could be sent to Ukraine, according to the GAO. In January 2024, the Pentagon paused shipments under the PDA program until Congress could provide the money to replace what had been sent. Congress eventually approved $13.4 billion in replenishment funds that April, and the PDA shipments resumed. Meanwhile, more munitions had begun to flow to Israel in October 2023, after Hamas had launched a brutal assault, taking more than 200 hostages, and Israel had responded by attacking Gaza. The Biden administration had set up a new system for arms transfers to Israel, largely avoiding the PDA. During the first six months of that effort, the United States made 42 deliveries totaling some 4 million munitions to Israel, according to the Pentagon inspector general’s office. This covered everything from artillery shells to guided missiles. I n 2024, a young Army Reserve lieutenant colonel named Sandra Thomas arrived in Washington to take a new job as the defense industrial base chief inside the office of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The depletion of missiles and munitions was, by then, an urgent issue. “There were munitions working groups stood up. It’s something that was briefed once a day to different generals,” Thomas told me. Thomas loves supply chains. She attended college on an ROTC scholarship, and once she was commissioned, she moved straight into logistics. When she left active duty in 2015, she became a supply-chain manager at a Michelin tire factory in South Carolina, a graduate-level crash course in corporate logistics. Thomas orchestrated the flow of crucial minerals, bead wires, and other components as they were fed into the factory, and helped organize the global delivery of finished tires. Then Thomas went back on active duty, and by 2020 she was the quartermaster in charge of the U.S. air base in Erbil, Iraq. She was like a city manager, overseeing a town of thousands in a place where summer temperatures can top 110 degrees Fahrenheit. But even for someone like Thomas, the U.S. missile supply chain proved frustrating. She was assigned to a team that tried to figure out how the Pentagon could buy all the missiles it needed for the future. The missiles were made by some of the largest and most profitable defense contractors in the world, but those companies were in no position to ramp up production. “They can’t go anywhere. They have no room to surge,” Thomas said. The Joint Chiefs’ office studied the issue for months, and the results were sobering. Pentagon analysts had set hypothetical targets for increased production of missiles such as the Patriot, the THAAD, and the JASSM. The idea was to see what it might take to expand assembly lines, replenish stockpiles, and have munitions to share with allies. For many common missile systems, doubling production or even boosting it by 60 percent would cost tens of billions of dollars up front. More concerning, even if the funding were available, hitting that increased rate of production would take three years to six and a half years for some missiles. A Pentagon study from 2018 helped explain why. America’s defense industry faced “an unprecedented set of challenges,” the report concluded. The missiles were powerful, but the defense industrial base that made them was fragile. The industry had consolidated to the point that just two companies received 97 percent of the missile spending. If those companies had a problem, it became the Pentagon’s problem. These prime contractors relied, in turn, on small manufacturers that had been hurt by the economics of deindustrialization. Just one company in the United States made a vital rocket-fuel chemical called ammonium perchlorate, creating a dangerous single point of failure. If the Pentagon wanted to boost production, it would somehow need to reach back into the supply chain to address these problems. Thomas and her team met with defense-industry officials and asked them about their supply chains. The top defense contractors were well aware of the problems with missile production; they had been openly talking about them for years. “The tragedy of Ukraine has unveiled some issues and weaknesses for our national-defense enterprise more broadly,” Lockheed Martin CEO James Taiclet told investment analysts during a conference call in 2023. In a later call, he likened the situation to a Dirty Harry movie, where the hero is in danger of running out of bullets. Taiclet told investors in 2024 that Lockheed was trying to address “fragility” in the missile-production system. “We’ve taken an all-hands-on-deck approach where we’ve seen the issues become more significant,” he said. Thomas was less than impressed with their efforts. She often crossed paths with defense contractors at war games and conferences. When she pressed the defense companies on plans to expand their factories, she mostly encountered roadblocks. They said they couldn’t share proprietary technology with subcontractors, for instance, and couldn’t afford to build a new assembly line unless they had long-term contracts to lock in demand or up-front payments to fund the expansion. But the same companies were simultaneously doling out generous cash payments to their shareholders in an effort to keep stock prices high. Lockheed Martin, for example, gave $6.8 billion back to shareholders in the form of dividends and stock buybacks in 2024 alone, while RTX gave its shareholders $3.7 billion that year. Thomas rotated out of her job in the Joint Chiefs’ office in July 2025. She was discouraged. Despite the big problems with missile production, the system seemed to be locked in stasis. “I think we’ve identified the problem, but we definitely can’t stop continuing to solve it,” she told me at the time. But, she said, as bad as things were, it still wasn’t the worst-case scenario: “I think that we haven’t hit rock bottom, for sure.” Seven months later, President Trump launched Operation Epic Fury. In this U.S. Navy released handout, Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. (DDG 121) fires a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile during operations in support of Operation Epic Fury, on February 28, 2026 at Sea. ( U.S. Navy / Getty) T here are 11 THAAD batteries in the world . The United States owns eight, the UAE owns two, and the Saudis have activated one, according to the Saudi Press Agency. (Saudi Arabia has purchased additional batteries, but only one has been reported as active.) At least five THAAD batteries were based in the Middle East in February 2026. Three of those belonged to the Emiratis and Saudis. In April 2025, Israeli media confirmed that a second THAAD battery was delivered to Israel. Another U.S. THAAD battery was moved to Jordan, where there is a major Jordanian base hosting U.S. forces. Each battery holds 48 interceptor missiles. The U.S. government does not disclose the locations of THAAD batteries, or how many backup missiles are kept in stockpiles in the region. The United States and Israel launched a joint attack on Iran on February 28, hitting more than 7,000 targets in the first few weeks. The U.S. has not released specific figures on how many munitions it used before the cease-fire in April, or on the level of stockpiles remaining. But outside analysts have formulated their own estimates. The United States used more than 11,000 munitions, costing $26 billion, in the first 16 days of the conflict, according to the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a British think tank. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that the United States used 1,060 to 1,430 Patriot interceptors before the cease-fire, amounting to more than half of the prewar stockpile. Based on reporting in The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal , CSIS calculates that the U.S. used 1,000 Tomahawk missiles and roughly 1,100 JASSM missiles, depleting those stockpiles by a third and a quarter, respectively. The THAAD missile was one of the most important of all the American and allied munitions, and it was used promiscuously. More than 150 THAADs were used during the 12-day war of 2025, according to CSIS, while 190 to 290 were used during Operation Epic Fury. CSIS estimates that the United States had only 452 THAAD interceptors left at the beginning of that operation. More interceptors have likely been delivered this year, however. The CSIS estimates that the current U.S. stockpile contains roughly 250 THAAD interceptors. One truth revealed about the THAAD this year is that it works quite well. The system knocked out ballistic missiles in the upper atmosphere with impressive reliability. But a second truth revealed about the THAAD was that it was facing a threat for which it was not well designed. The Iranians employed a new form of warfare that military analysts call “precision mass,” combining the threat of a limited number of precision-guided missiles—a technology perfected and dominated by the United States since the Cold War—with the power of cheap drones and ballistic missiles. The THAAD interceptors, which cost $12 million, were used to shoot down Iranian missiles like the Ghadr, which costs an estimated $5 million. Iran had been building these missiles for years, and it was able to send waves of them, depleting the reserves of THAAD interceptors. Iran also fired a newer generation of missile, called the Khorramshahr-4, that can maneuver on its final descent, making it more difficult for a THAAD to hit. While these missiles rained down from the upper atmosphere, Iran simultaneously dispatched large numbers of Shahed drones, which cost $20,000 to $50,000 apiece. The THAAD is no good against Shaheds, and the Patriot missiles are too scarce to waste in shooting them down. Countries like the UAE scrambled to knock down Shaheds by using attack helicopters and expensive air-to-air missiles fired from jets. Iran attacked the UAE with particular ferocity. On March 3, Iran launched 186 ballistic missiles and 812 attack drones at the Emirates, according to Axios . Several dozen drones and only one ballistic missile made it through, according to Emirati officials, but the attack strained the U.S. system that was envisioned back in 2007, which tied together the THAAD and Patriot interceptors. At the start of the war, debris from Iranian drones hit the international airport in Abu Dhabi and the luxury Fairmont hotel in Dubai. Images of the flames and smoke were shared on social media, damaging the Emirates’ hard-won reputation as an oasis of peace and prosperity. The Dubai International Airport, a global transit hub, was also hit that day, and attacked again on March 7 and 11. On March 10, Iranian drones struck a large oil refinery in the remote town of Ruwais, causing a fire and shutting down production. At least three foreign workers were killed in the Emirates in the early days of the war. One of them, a Pakistani driver named Murib Zaman, was reportedly killed by falling debris from an intercepted missile. Similar attacks unfolded across the region, in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, and Israel. In the Israeli towns of Arad and Dimona, Iranian ballistic missiles made it through the air-defense system on March 21, at a time when the Israeli military was triaging scarce interceptors, according to analysts. When critics attacked Reagan’s “Star Wars” program in the 1980s, they said the idea of a missile-defense shield rested on a fallacy: A missile shield needed to work perfectly, all the time, or it effectively wouldn’t work at all. If just one or two nuclear missiles made it through, the value of the entire endeavor would be undercut. The shield would have done little more than provide a false sense of security. A similar logic applied to the Middle East this year. When Mohamed bin Zayed considered purchasing the THAAD, he characterized the decision in near-existential terms, according to a State Department summary of his comments. “MbZ recognizes that partnership with the US is fundamental to the UAE’s continued success,” a 2009 State Department cable reads, “but he also knows that the relationship is controversial among his people, and that if the U.S. is perceived as an unreliable protector, his own power base will erode.” That raw calculus is now driving strategic reassessments across the region. U.S. military bases, once considered protective shields, now look more like targets. Large investments in U.S. weapons systems are being recalculated for their value against precision mass. Alliances built over years are up for renegotiation—in May, the United Arab Emirates left the OPEC oil cartel in a bid for more independence, dealing a blow to regional alliances. [ Brynn Tannehill: The dangerous mismatch between American missiles and Iranian drones ] The United States’ inability to rapidly defeat Iran or to fully protect its allies could have far-reaching effects on the U.S. position in the Middle East, Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told me. The Middle East has played a pivotal role in the U.S.-dominated economic system that has existed since World War II. The primary U.S. strategic interest in the region was to keep oil flowing to global markets, powering the global economy. U.S. military bases and interventions ensured that this system survived, Wertheim said. If those bases are abandoned or U.S. allies drift away, the entire system could be at risk. “We could be moving away from a Middle East that can be fairly described as being an American-dominated region,” Wertheim said. And the damage to America’s reputation will hardly be limited to that region. “For roughly the rest of the Trump administration, we will be running an experiment where the United States is significantly less capable in its defensive capabilities on a global basis,” Wertheim said, as munitions stockpiles continue to dwindle. After a pause in May, the United States and Iran resumed hostilities this summer. On July 17, an Iranian missile penetrated U.S. air defenses and killed three U.S. soldiers stationed at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, in Jordan. All three soldiers were assigned to air-defense units, and the base was home to a U.S. THAAD battery. It’s not clear if the THAAD was even deployed during the attack. The Iranians had borrowed tactics the Russians had developed in the Ukraine war, battering U.S. air defenses with a mix of drones and missiles. Seth Jones, an analyst with CSIS, published an essay in the The Wall Street Journal warning that the U.S. had been “slow to learn” the lessons of warfare in the age of precision mass. Jones recommended that the U.S. military begin acting more Ukrainian. It can erect anti-drone nets and concrete barriers, install drone-jamming devices, and dig new underground bunkers. It’s hardly the stuff of science fiction, like the THAAD. But it just might keep service members alive.

items.title: La alerta roja por lluvia en Cataluña obliga a suspender trenes AVE, parte del Metro y cortar la Ronda de Dalt
items.description: Cataluña vive una jornada con una alerta roja meteorológica activada por fuertes lluvias en buena parte del litoral y el prelitoral, unas lluvias que podrían dejar hasta 180 litros por metro cuadrado. Protección Civil de la Generalitat envió ayer un mensaje EsAlert a los habitantes de nueve comarcas, entre ellas las más pobladas de Cataluña, para pedir precaución, aunque no ha establecido medidas concretas de restricción de movilidad. Las horas centrales del día serán las que más lluvia puedan registrar según las previsiones del MeteoCat. Los principales problemas esta mañana son en las líneas ferroviarias. Renfe ha suspendido varios servicios de la Alta Velocidad entre las 9 y las 11, así como diferentes trenes de media distancia. Durante la mañana, la Guardia Urbana de Barcelona ha cortado la Ronda de Dalt en sentido Llobregat a la altura del paseo Vall d’Hebron por inundación. Además, Transportes Metropolitanos de Barcelona (TMB) ha tenido que suspender el servicio de metro de parte de la L4, L5 y L11. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Megabarcos de pesca: ¿son realmente más dañinos para los océanos?
items.description: ¿Hay un tamaño a partir del cual se deba considerar un barco pesquero demasiado grande? La organización Bloom , una asociación francesa de defensa del océano, ha publicado este martes un informe en el que propone un límite para las embarcaciones de pesca europeas : 33 metros. Aunque en la flota pesquera de la UE hay buques descomunales que superan los 100 metros de eslora, esta entidad conservacionista considera que todos los barcos de 33 metros o más son ya demasiado grandes para garantizar el futuro de la pesca y de los propios pescadores, y van en contra de la “seguridad alimentaria” y la “soberanía económica de los territorios”. items.title: Cameroun-MRC : pourquoi ‘’l’autorisation’’ du 28 septembre change tout après Kamto et Mota
items.description: © MRC L'obtention du récépissé N°000332 pour la convention du 17 octobre n'est pas une simple formalité administrative. C'est la première victoire politique de l'après-Kamto, et elle dit beaucoup sur la stratégie de survie du MRC. Pendant 10 mois, le MRC vivait dans une fiction juridique. Le ministre de l’Administration territoriale -Minat, le 19 août dernier, avait été clair. Il ne reconnaît plus rien depuis la 3ème convention ordinaire des 9 et 10 décembre 2023. Tout ce qui a été fait après - y compris la visioconférence du 21 décembre 2025 qui avait reconduit Maurice Kamto - est frappé de nullité à ses yeux. Par conséquent, le parti était comme sans direction légalement reconnue, puis décapité par deux démissions coup sur coup, celle du président Maurice Kamto et celle de son numéro 1 historique Mamadou Mota. Dans ce vide, qui pouvait parler au nom du MRC ? Le Minat a répondu indirectement ce 28 septembre : il faut choisir la personne. Mais avant, la démarche suivie pour obtenir le récépissé n’est pas anodine. Le choix de l'homme qui dépose la demande est un message juridique Ce n'est pas Tiriane Balbine Noah la présidente par intérim qui dépose. C'est Justin Roger Noah, Secrétaire Général Adjoint n°1. Il est issu de la dernière direction reconnue par le Minat, celle de décembre 2023. En acceptant son dossier, le sous-préfet de Yaoundé IV, et à travers lui le Minat qui publie le récépissé sur sa page, reconnaît de facto qu'il est un interlocuteur légitime. C'est une rupture avec novembre 2025, où ce même arrondissement avait interdit la convention de Kamto. Cette fois, l'administration dit oui. Cela signifie qu'elle considère que la démarche de l'équipe intérimaire rentre dans la légalité de 2023, pas dans l'illégalité de 2025. Pour Tiriane Noah, présidente par intérim, c'est une légitimation par procuration. Elle ne pouvait pas déposer elle-même sans que le Minat ne conteste sa qualité. Elle passe par le SGA1, qui lui, est inattaquable sur le plan administratif. Fin de la stratégie de la chaise vide Après les démissions, deux options s'offraient au MRC. La première était le pourrissement. Rester dans la contestation de la décision du 19 août, crier à l'acharnement, et ne pas tenir de convention. La deuxième était le réalisme. Revenir à la case départ légale de 2023, et refaire tout le processus dans les règles exigées par le Minat pour exister à nouveau. Tiriane Noah et ceux qui l’entourent ont choisi l'option 2. Sa tournée à Ngaoundéré et Garoua ce week-end, l'installation d'un bureau régional, la présentation d'une liste pour le 17 octobre, et maintenant ce récépissé, sont les étapes d'une même stratégie qui vise à reconstruire la légalité par le bas. Le soutien de Mamadou Mota, devenu coordonnateur de sa campagne, est essentiel dans ce schéma. Mota était l'autre démissionnaire. En revenant comme parrain, il colmate la fracture morale laissée par les départs et évite que le MRC ne soit perçu comme un parti abandonné par ses chefs. Le vrai test de la convention du 17 octobre Avoir ‘’l'autorisation’’ de tenir la convention est une chose. Faire reconnaître son procès-verbal par le Minat en est une autre. C'est là que tout s'est bloqué en décembre 2025. Le parti avait tenu sa convention malgré l'interdiction, et le Minat avait refusé de reconnaître les résolutions. Cette fois, si la convention du 17 octobre se tient à Odza, sans incident, et que le procès-verbal est déposé avec deux listes concurrentes annoncées, Tiriane Balbine Noah et Pierre Emmanuel Binyam, le Minat sera obligé de se prononcer. S'il reconnaît le PV, le MRC renaît légalement et pourra investir des candidats pour les législatives et municipales de 2027. S'il refuse à nouveau, le parti retombera dans le vide juridique, mais cette fois, il ne pourra plus accuser l'administration de l'avoir empêché de se réunir. Le récépissé du 28 septembre n'est pas la fin de la crise du MRC. C'est la fin de l'excuse administrative. Après Kamto et Mota, Tiriane Noah a obtenu le droit de jouer. Maintenant, elle doit gagner le match du 17 octobre. La seule menace qui plane encore sur cette convention, est une éventuelle décision judiciaire découlant d’une saisine de l’un des anciens membres exclus, en particulier Thierry Okala Ebode et Willy Mengue. Cet article Cameroun-MRC : pourquoi ‘’l'autorisation’’ du 28 septembre change tout après Kamto et Mota est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Économie russe : en 2027, la Russie de Poutine dépensera plus que jamais pour la guerre
items.description: Selon les documents joints au projet de budget fédéral auxquels Reuters a eu accès, Moscou prévoit de consacrer 17 100 milliards de roubles à la défense en 2027, ce qui équivaut à environ 178 milliards d'euros au taux de change actuel Russia raises 2027 military spending by 27 %, budget documents show », Reuters , 28 septembre 2026.'> 1 . Il s’agirait d’une hausse de 32 % par rapport à 2026 (environ 134 milliards d’euros) Россия в 2027 году намерена потратить на оборону на 27 % больше первоначального плана — Reuters », Dojd , 28 septembre 2026.'> 2 et près du triple du budget des forces armées françaises pour 2027 (63,4 milliards d’euros). Le gouvernement doit présenter le projet de budget à la Douma avant le 1er octobre, mais son adoption n’est qu’une simple formalité, l’assemblée fonctionnant comme une chambre d’enregistrement . Depuis les élections de septembre, le parti de Poutine « Russie unie » détient 355 des 450 sièges, soit bien plus que la majorité constitutionnelle (300 sièges). Les autres partis représentés appartiennent à « l’opposition systémique » qui soutient la guerre. Selon Reuters , le gouvernement a revu à la hausse ses prévisions de déficit pour 2026, les portant de 1,6 % à 3,2 % du PIB. L'effort de guerre est donc de plus en plus financé par la dette, ce qui présente des risques systémiques pour la tenue de l’économie russe. Les intérêts s’élèvent à près de 4 000 milliards de roubles par an, soit environ 10 % des dépenses fédérales – plus que les dépenses consacrées à l’Éducation et à la Santé réunies Russia Has a Budget Problem. Borrowing Its Way Out Won't Be So Simple », The Moscow Times , 28 septembre 2026.'> 3 . Privé d’investisseurs étrangers en raison des sanctions, l’État dépend des banques russes, qui ne disposent plus de liquidités suffisantes pour racheter sa dette. Le directeur financier de la Sberbank, Taras Skvortsov, l’exprimait ainsi en juillet : « Aujourd’hui, les banques ne disposent de fonds que pour accorder des prêts à leurs clients » Russian Banks Lack Cash to Buy Government Debt, Sberbank Executive Says », The Moscow Times , 31 juillet 2026.'> 4 . La Banque centrale maintient son taux directeur à 14 %. Elle prévient qu’un déficit plus important que prévu exigerait une politique monétaire « plus restrictive », au détriment de l’investissement Банк России принял решение сохранить ключевую ставку на уровне 14,00 % годовых , Banque centrale russe, 11 septembre 2026.'> 5 . Plusieurs nouvelles taxes ont été annoncées, le gouvernement s’attendant par exemple à récupérer 200 milliards de roubles par an sur les bénéfices exceptionnels des entreprises du secteur métallurgique et minier. Selon l’économiste Vladislav Inozemtsev , « cette année, la Russie consacrera très probablement plus de 10 % de son PIB à des fins militaires pour la première fois depuis l’époque soviétique ». L’article Économie russe : en 2027, la Russie de Poutine dépensera plus que jamais pour la guerre est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards woo US voters with open letter
items.description: (Removes 'Hold' from headline) DUBAI, Sept 29 (Reuters) - Iran's Revolutionary Guards, whose power and influence have expanded since the US and Israel pursued war against Iran, have appealed to US midterm voters to reject President Donald Trump's policies and accept an offer of peaceful coexistence. The assertions were made on Tuesday in a 25-page open letter addressed to the American people, urging them to oppose US support for Israel and foreign wars and arguing that Iran and the US could coexist if US policy changed.

items.title: Législatives 2026 : géographie du vote, bastions électoraux et fracture de la participation
items.description: Au terme du scrutin législatif du 23 septembre 2026, la nouvelle cartographie électorale du Royaume révèle une dynamique territoriale à deux vitesses. Si la répartition globale des 395 sièges consacre la victoire du Parti Authenticité et Modernité (PAM) avec 97 députés, la lecture régionale des résultats met en lumière des écarts saisissants de mobilisation citoyenne et des ancrages partisans bien différenciés. Le Sud en tête de la mobilisation, ancrage affirmé de l'Istiqlal Les provinces sahariennes confirment leur statut de réservoir majeur de participation citoyenne. Les régions de Laâyoune-Sakia El Hamra et de Dakhla-Oued Ed-Dahab affichent les taux de participation les plus élevés du pays, franchissant le seuil des 60 % le jour du vote. Sur le plan politique, le Parti de l'Istiqlal (PI) s'impose comme la force hégémonique dans ces deux régions, consolidant ses bastions historiques dans le Sahara marocain. Dans la zone de transition de Guelmim-Oued Noun, où l'affluence aux urnes est également restée soutenue, c'est le PAM qui décroche la première place. Souss et Centre : récompense du RNI et poussée rurale du PAM Dans la région de Souss-Massa, caractérisée par une participation moyenne-élevée tirée par les zones agricoles et périurbaines, le Rassemblement National des Indépendants (RNI) parvient à maintenir son leadership régional malgré un recul au niveau national. Plus au centre, dans les régions montagneuses et rurales de Béni Mellal-Khénifra et Drâa-Tafilalet, la participation s'est maintenue à un niveau intermédiaire, permettant au PAM de prendre la tête, suivi de près par le Mouvement Populaire (MP) et l'Istiqlal. Les métropoles du Nord et de l'Atlantique : abstention urbaine et reconquête du PJD Le contraste le plus saisissant provient des grands bassins démographiques du Nord et de l'axe Atlantique. Dans les régions de Casablanca-Settat (69 sièges) et Rabat-Salé-Kénitra (49 sièges), ainsi qu'à Fès-Meknès, Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceïma et dans L'Oriental, la participation s'est affaissée pour s'établir en dessous de la moyenne nationale (38,02 %). Cette désaffection urbaine n'a pas empêché le PAM d'arriver en tête en nombre global de voix et de sièges dans l'ensemble de ces régions nordiques et centrales. Toutefois, ces grandes agglomérations ont été le théâtre d'un rééquilibrage politique majeur : le Parti de la Justice et du Développement (PJD) y enregistre une remontée spectaculaire en s'imposant dans plusieurs métropoles clés (Rabat, Casablanca, Temara, Fès, Tanger), tandis que l'Alliance de la Gauche crée la surprise en effectuant une percée remarquée dans ces mêmes centres urbains. Une recomposition territoriale révélatrice des nouveaux équilibres Cette géographie électorale à deux visages confirme que le paysage politique marocain s'articule désormais autour d'une double réalité. D'un côté, les provinces du Sud et les zones rurales continuent de jouer un rôle de stabilisateur institutionnel, caractérisées par un civisme électoral élevé et la primauté des partis traditionnels de la majorité. De l'autre, les métropoles urbaines expriment une insatisfaction grandissante par une abstention record, tout en servant de terrain de reconquête pour l'opposition parlementaire et les forces émergentes. Outre la victoire comptable du PAM au niveau national, le véritable enjeu de la législature à venir résidera dans la capacité des élus à combler cette fracture territoriale et citoyenne. La gouvernance locale et la redistribution socio-économique dans les grands centres urbains constitueront les tests décisifs pour une majorité réaménagée, face à des villes qui ont clairement signifié leur volonté de rééquilibrer le débat politique. The post Législatives 2026 : géographie du vote, bastions électoraux et fracture de la participation appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: 5 000 collaborateurs, 5 000 arbres : quand la croissance devient un engagement
items.description: À l’occasion du franchissement du cap des 5000 collaborateurs, ASM a choisi d’associer cette étape de son développement à un engagement concret en faveur de l’environnement : planter 5000 arbres chaque année jusqu’en 2030, soit 25 000 arbres sur cinq ans. Le 24 septembre 2026, cet engagement a pris forme dans la région de Khémisset, avec une première opération de plantation menée aux côtés de High Atlas Foundation. Le leadership donne le coup d’envoi Plus de 100 cadres supérieurs d’ASM se sont mobilisés sur le terrain pour lancer cette initiative. Cette première journée a marqué le début d’une mobilisation appelée à s’étendre progressivement à l’ensemble des collaborateurs, qui prennent à leur tour le relais pour contribuer à l’objectif de 5000 arbres fixé pour 2026. Une dynamique collective qui traduit une philosophie claire : faire grandir l’entreprise, c’est aussi faire grandir son impact. Une initiative qui s’inscrit dans la durée Avec High Atlas Foundation, ASM inscrit cette démarche dans une approche structurée et ancrée dans le territoire, qui prend en compte le choix des sites et des espèces, les réalités environnementales locales, l’implication des communautés et le suivi du projet. Le 24 septembre a ainsi marqué le lancement d’un engagement appelé à se renouveler chaque année jusqu’en 2030. « Notre croissance doit aussi laisser une empreinte positive » : une ambition qui commence avec les cadres d’ASM et se prolonge avec la mobilisation de l’ensemble des collaborateurs. Pour marquer cette étape symbolique des 5 000 collaborateurs, ASM organisera également une soirée réunissant ses collaborateurs, pensée comme un moment de célébration et de partage autour de ce cap collectif, et comme l’occasion de faire vivre les valeurs qui accompagnent cette nouvelle étape de son développement. items.title: Más de un tercio de las mujeres con hijos tiene menos de los deseados: “Las condiciones óptimas llegan muy tarde”
items.description: La brecha de fecundidad. Ese es el gran problema para los expertos. Que se quiera tener hijos y no se pueda; o que se tengan menos de los que se desearía. Y en España, casi el 35% de las mujeres con descendencia tiene menos niños de los que querría, según el avance de los resultados de la encuesta de fecundidad publicado este martes por el Instituto Nacional de Estadística. Un dato que permanece bastante estable respecto a 2018 (solo cinco décimas menos), la última vez que se elaboró este sondeo . Las cifras dibujan un país en el que se van retrasando las transiciones vitales. La edad a la que emanciparse; a la que se encuentra la pareja adecuada; en la que se consigue un buen trabajo. “Las condiciones que se consideran óptimas para tener hijos llegan muy tarde”, explica Mariona Lozano, demógrafa del Centro de Estudios Demográficos de la Universidad Autónoma de Barcelona. Así que la gran mayoría preferiría tener dos hijos (siete de cada 10 mujeres), pero de media se tienen 1,1, según los últimos datos disponibles, de 2024. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Grève en France : risque de perturbations des vols vers l’Algérie ce mardi
items.description: Les vols entre l’Algérie et la France pourraient connaître des perturbations ce mardi 29 septembre à cause d’une grève dans la fonction publique française. Selon l’AFP, les organisations syndicales représentatives de la fonction publique préparent une journée de grève mardi, pour protester contre un nouveau gel du point d'indice. Le débrayage concerne aussi les fonctionnaires des aéroports. Vols réduits à Paris-Roissy et Marseille-Provence En prévision de cette grève, la Direction générale de l'aviation civile (DGAC) a demandé aux compagnies aériennes de réduire leurs programmes de vols dans plusieurs aéroports français, dont ceux de Roissy (Paris) et de Marseille, afin de “limiter les perturbations et garantir la sécurité des opérations aériennes”. La DGAC a incité les compagnies à réduire leurs programmes de vols de 5 % à Roissy-Charles-de-Gaulle entre 07 h 00 et 20 h 00, et de 25 % à Marseille-Provence entre 16 h 00 et minuit. Ces deux aéroports assurent une grande partie des liaisons aériennes avec l’Algérie. Les compagnies desservant l'Algérie n’ont pas annoncé de perturbations Pour le moment, les compagnies desservant l’Algérie, notamment Air France, Air Algérie, Transavia et ASL Airlines, n’ont pas fait état d'annulation ou de report de vols. Outre Paris et Marseille, des perturbations pourraient en outre survenir “sur certains créneaux de la journée” dans les aéroports de Nantes-Atlantique, Strasbourg-Entzheim, Limoges, Tarbes-Lourdes-Pyrénées et Pau-Pyrénées, a précisé la direction de l’aviation civile, qui a invité les passagers à s'informer auprès de leur compagnie aérienne.
